title: ACC announces five million battery cells 'Made in France' - electrive.com
content:
The Automotive Cells Company (ACC) battery joint venture between Stellantis, Mercedes, and TotalEnergies has announced producing its five-millionth cell at its factory in France. The plant's second production block, with a capacity of 12.9 GWh, is set to begin production in 2027.
Image: ACC
At the Paris Motor Show, ACC announced that its current cell output at the Douvrin site is enough to equip nearly 40,000 vehicles with its own battery cells. The joint venture also revealed plans to commission the second production block at the plant next year to manufacture batteries for Mercedes-Benz electric vehicles. This will increase the site’s capacity by 12.9 GWh from next year, bringing the total to just under 26 GWh. The final expansion stage currently envisages three production blocks with a combined manufacturing capacity of around 40 GWh.
Automotive Cells Company (ACC) is one of the few European manufacturers of battery cells and modules for electric vehicles. Founded in 2020, the company develops and produces batteries based on NMC chemistry. Its shareholders are Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, and Saft, a subsidiary of TotalEnergies. ACC currently employs around 2,500 people in France, at its research and development centre and pilot plant in Nouvelle-Aquitaine, and in the Hauts-de-France metropolitan region where its gigafactory in Douvrin is located.
ACC batteries now in eight Stellantis EVs
Management emphasises that ACC has “grown significantly and its industrial maturity has evolved considerably” since the last motor show two years ago. The company’s cells and modules are now installed in eight premium electric car models, all marketed by the Stellantis Group. These include the Peugeot E-3008 and E-5008, Jeep Compass, Lancia Gamma, DS N° 7 and N° 8, Citroën C5 Aircross, and the Opel Grandland.
Allan Swan, CEO of ACC since May 2026, said: “Reaching 5 million cells produced in France is an important milestone for ACC and a clear demonstration of the progress achieved by our teams over the past years. It shows that Europe can develop and industrialise advanced battery technologies at scale.” Nevertheless, the challenge of competitiveness remains: “Europe must now ensure that its industrial ambitions are supported by a framework that enables battery manufacturing to compete on a level playing field. Only a competitive European offering will be able to meet the demand for ‘Made in the EU’ production,” Swan noted.
“Defect rates are approaching target levels”
This comes against the backdrop of the EU’s debated draft of the
Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA)
and its “Made in Europe” aspirations. Swan hopes for swift implementation of the IAA, which would “provide the necessary support to boost demand for batteries manufactured in Europe.” However, there are also voices expressing concerns that the EU industry
may not even be able to meet its own battery demand
Regardless of industrial policy guidelines, ACC still faces its own challenges, primarily the high defect rate in cell and module production. The company’s interim report states: “Defect rates are steadily approaching target levels.” It also notes: “ACC is successfully supplying Stellantis in accordance with the agreed production schedules.”
Stellantis struggles with battery shortages
This contrasts with reports from around two weeks ago, when
and the German trade publication
Handelsblatt
reported at the end of September that Stellantis would temporarily halt production at its French plants in Sochaux, Rennes, and Mulhouse for at least one week each. In two cases, this was due to shortages in the supply of EV batteries from ACC.
However, the pause is only indirectly related to the shortage of ACC’s large nickel-based batteries. Stellantis primarily aims to avoid producing too many other vehicles “to prevent building up inventories that do not match customer demand,” as the company explained. After all, demand is particularly high for the long-range electric models (equipped with ACC batteries) for which customers currently face very long waiting periods.
The Sochaux plant in eastern France, which produces models such as the Peugeot 3008 and Peugeot 5008, is set to pause operations from 23 to 30 October. The Rennes factory, which manufactures the Citroën C5 Aircross among others, will close from 22 to 30 October. The previously announced production halt in Mulhouse from 15 to 30 October is said to have other reasons unrelated to battery shortages.
ACC’s supplies have been experiencing a tight bottleneck for Stellantis production for some time now. The joint venture originally planned to build three plants in France, Germany, and Italy but is now focusing on ramping up its only cell factory in Douvrin, France. The other two major projects
were scrapped
Ramp-up has proven challenging
Bloomberg
reported in February, citing internal sources, operations in Douvrin have also faced difficulties. At the beginning of the year, ACC was reportedly only able to equip around 1,000 cars per month with long-range batteries, far below its original target. The joint venture is said to have subsequently brought in a team of experts from China to boost production and reduce high defect rates. In February, ACC also acknowledged fundamental issues: ACC Secretary-General Matthieu Hubert told
Bloomberg
at the time that the ramp-up was proving challenging.
Stellantis uses the battery cells from ACC’s Douvrin plant in the aforementioned EVs based on the STLA Medium platform. For these vehicles with ACC cells,
Bloomberg
already reported delivery delays of up to eight months in February.
Long-range models face very long delivery times
In April, a report by the German automotive trade publication
Automobilwoche
followed, stating that
private customers in particular are facing very long waits for their long-range models
, specifically focusing on the Opel Grandland, Peugeot E-3008, and E-5008. A Stellantis dealer told the trade journal at the time that deliveries had been pushed back to the first or second quarter of 2027. Other dealers reportedly received no binding delivery dates at all.
The situation remains delicate for Stellantis brands. After all, it only affects customers willing to pay nearly €5,000 more for a larger battery with 97 kWh instead of 73 kWh capacity and the corresponding range increase, compared to the same model with a smaller battery.
Meanwhile, ACC is said to have reduced defect rates and further stabilised production. However, a Stellantis spokesperson told
that they are still not receiving enough batteries, even though ACC has made significant progress in production, in the context of the announced plant pauses. Demand for long-range models, particularly from fleet customers, remains high and continues to exceed current supply.

title: Seres commits Aito to CATL batteries long-term - electrive.com
content:
CATL and Seres want to secure their long-term collaboration on batteries for the Aito automotive brand. To accomodate the according demand, the battery making giant is increasing its production capacity in Chongqing to more than 20 GWh per year. Fast charging, battery services, and expansion into foreign markets are also part of the agreement.
Aito 9 in Paris
Image: Aito
Chinese battery manufacturer CATL has announced that the Aito brand, a collaboration between Seres and Huawei, will continue to use CATL batteries across its entire model range. Both companies also aim to deepen their collaboration in battery production, charging infrastructure, battery services, and the development of international markets.
The companies signed the agreement on 10 October at Seres’ headquarters in Chongqing. Aito’s battery electric and range-extended combustion models have been equipped with CATL batteries and will now continue to do so long term. The brand’s cumulative deliveries have now exceeded 1.2 million vehicles, but the companies did not disclose financial details or the duration of the new agreement.
CATL and Seres to expand battery assembly
A key focus of the cooperation is expanding battery production using the factory-in-factory concept. CATL already
operates a battery assembly plant on the premises
of the Seres Super Factory in Chongqing, which is now set for expansion. The second phase of construction is planned to have an annual production capacity of 10 to 12 GWh. Once completed, the combined capacity of both phases will exceed 20 GWh per year. This proximity between battery system manufacturing and vehicle assembly is expected to streamline industrial processes and enhance cost competitiveness.
The first phase of the project began operation in mid-2025. At that time, CATL commissioned two production lines for battery packs based on its Cell-to-Pack (CTP 2.0) technology. The Chongqing site was also CATL’s first production base in the city and its first project following the “plant-in-plant” principle. The newly agreed second phase will correspondingly expand production capacities for Aito.
Cooperation also covers charging and battery services
Beyond battery supply, CATL and Seres aim to expand their collaboration in fast charging and battery services. According to CATL, the goal is to offer a service portfolio that covers the entire battery lifecycle, but the companies have not yet provided specific details on the services, locations, or timelines involved, and their public statements on this remain entirely non-specific.
Another component of the agreement is the joint development of foreign markets, with the partners explicitly mentioning Europe, the Middle East, and Central Asia. Whether and how they plan to establish joint charging offerings, battery services, or other activities in these regions remains unclear for now. Last year, Aito announced its intention to
export three electric vehicles
to the global market, and the
launch in the United Arab Emirates has already taken place
. It is expected that Aito will also outline its plans for Europe at this week’s Paris Motor Show.
CATL secures long-term supply relationship
For CATL, the agreement means continuing its existing supply relationship with a growing Chinese automotive brand in the long term, while further integrating production into vehicle manufacturing. Seres, for its part, secures the continued supply of CATL batteries for its Aito model range.
The agreement follows another significant partnership for Aito. At the end of September, Seres and Huawei also signed a
new five-year cooperation agreement for the brand
. The collaboration with Huawei focuses on advancing the Aito business, while CATL continues to play a central role in battery supply.
Aito was founded at the end of 2021 by Huawei and Seres and is now part of the Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance (HIMA), which Huawei has established with various automakers. In addition to Aito, the HIMA ecosystem includes
(with Chery),
(with BAIC),
(with JAC), and
(with SAIC).

title: Circuland helps the battery industry prepare for the EU Battery Passport - Batteries News
content:
Circuland supports battery manufacturers and importers preparing for the February 2027 EU Battery Passport deadline.
Circuland’s Battery Passport platform helps battery manufacturers and importers bring together product and supplier data, identify information gaps, and create and maintain digital records for individual batteries.
Circuland supports preparation by connecting information from existing systems through APIs and configured integrations, generating unique identifiers and QR codes, and helping organisations manage passport data throughout the battery’s lifecycle.
The requirement applies regardless of where the battery was manufactured. With the deadline approaching, manufacturers and importers need to establish how they will collect the required information, create passports for individual batteries and maintain those records throughout their lifecycle.
A Battery Passport is an electronic record linked to an individual battery through a unique identifier and accessed using a QR code. It contains required information about the battery’s identity, composition, performance and lifecycle, with different access rights for public and restricted information.
The Commission’s guidance identifies which data points apply to each battery category from February 2027. Not every field is mandatory for every battery, and some information becomes required only when the underlying obligations apply. Required information must be accurate, complete and up to date, including relevant updates during use and changes in battery status.
The framework is now taking shape
The implementation picture has become much clearer in recent months:
References to six harmonised horizontal Digital Product Passport standards were published through Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/1736. Further technical specifications, including on security and authentication, may still evolve.
The EU Digital Product Passport Registry and its testing environment launched on 20 July 2026. Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1778, which establishes the Registry, entered into force on 6 August 2026.
Version 2.0 of the Commission’s guidance on Battery Passport data points, dated 15 August 2026, was announced by the Commission on 21 August 2026.
Organisations can already prepare their Registry access and verification, although the Commission’s current user guide states that Battery Passport registration cannot yet be completed because the battery semantic catalogue is still under development. With the deadline approaching, the practical question for companies is no longer what a Battery Passport is, but whether their data, processes and systems are ready to support one.
The challenge: data spread across the value chain
The economic operator placing the battery on the EU market or putting it into service is responsible for ensuring that required passport information is accurate, complete and up to date. Practical tasks may be delegated through written authorisation, but this does not transfer ultimate legal responsibility.
The information needed is often spread across ERP, PLM, sustainability systems and supplier records. Organisations therefore need a repeatable process for mapping existing data to passport requirements, collecting missing information and maintaining individual battery records as relevant data changes.
How Circuland helps
Circuland is a Battery Passport platform built for the EU Batteries Regulation, covering EV, LMT and industrial batteries. It builds on the team’s experience developing and implementing digital product and building passports in the construction sector.
Circuland connects information from existing systems through APIs and configured integrations. Teams can use available product and supplier data to start passport records, identify missing information and generate identifiers and QR codes for individual batteries. Configured connections can support subsequent updates from source systems.
The platform supports the passport preparation and management process. Compliance also depends on the accuracy and completeness of the supplied data, fulfilment of applicable regulatory requirements and successful Registry registration.
Standards-aligned identification:
unique identifiers and print-ready QR codes aligned with the harmonised Digital Product Passport standards, for organisations with or without GS1 membership.
Long-term continuity:
Battery Passports can be hosted on the company’s own domain, so printed QR codes can stay stable over the battery’s life.
Lifecycle and access control:
Battery Passports can be updated as a battery’s status changes, with public information for everyone and restricted data only for authorised parties.
Accessible across Europe:
available in all official EU languages, with accessibility options for both operators and the public.
Learn more:
https://circuland.co.uk
About Circuland
Circuland is a UK technology company providing digital product and building passport software. Its platform helps organisations structure, share and maintain product and asset information throughout their lifecycle. Its Battery Passport offering supports manufacturers and importers preparing for Regulation (EU) 2023/1542.

title: Smart #2 revives the electric Fortwo with 290 km of range for €19,990
content:
Fred Lambert
| Oct 12 2026 - 8:12 am PT
The Smart #2 Premium. Image: smart
Smart is back in the two-seater business. The Mercedes-Benz and Geely joint venture unveiled the all-electric Smart #2 at the Paris Motor Show today, with a 35.8 kWh LFP battery, up to 290 km (180 miles) of WLTP range, and a starting price of €19,990.
That’s more than double the range of the last Smart EQ Fortwo, which never got DC fast charging. Early orders open in Europe tomorrow, and deliveries start in 2027.
The Fortwo formula, with the EV problems fixed
Smart picked the same Paris show where it revealed its first two-seater concept 30 years ago, and it didn’t mess with the recipe. The #2 is 2,746 mm long, about 5 cm longer than the old EQ Fortwo. The wheels are still pushed out to the corners, and the two-tone paint and split tailgate are back.
The turning circle is 6.95 meters curb-to-curb. Tiny.
The split tailgate carries over from the Fortwo. Image: smart
The big change is underneath. Smart developed a new platform for the car, which it calls Electric Compact Architecture (ECA), with the battery in the floor and a 60 kW motor driving the rear wheels with 130 Nm of torque. The company also claims the #2 has the first five-link rear suspension in its class.
The new Electric Compact Architecture (ECA) platform under the Smart #2. Image: smart
Here’s how it compares to the car it replaces. Power is identical. Almost everything else isn’t:
Smart EQ Fortwo (2020-2024)
Smart #2 (2027)
17.6 kWh
35.8 kWh LFP
WLTP range
290 km (target)
DC fast charging
AC charging

EQ Fortwo figures from EV Database. Smart #2 figures from smart, pending EU homologation.
On a DC fast charger, Smart says the #2 goes from 10 to 80% in about 20 minutes. The base Pure trim is stuck with a 7.4 kW single-phase onboard charger, which takes about 5 hours for the same session, while the other trims get 11 kW. There’s also vehicle-to-load, but you need to buy a separate adapter for it.
The Smart #2 cabin, with an 8.8-inch driver display and a 10.1-inch center screen. Image: smart
Inside, there’s a bench-style seat layout, a 10.1-inch center screen, an 8.8-inch driver display, and an eight-year connectivity package. Adaptive cruise control with stop-and-go and Smart’s Pilot Assist are standard on every trim.
Four trims, starting at €19,990
Here’s the German pricing Smart released this afternoon. It says the €19,990 starting price also applies in France and Italy:
Pure: €19,990
Pure+: €20,990 (11 kW AC charging, heated driver seat)
Premium: €24,490 (glass roof, heated faux-leather seats, 7-speaker Sennheiser system)
Couture Edition: €25,690 (limited to 999 units in Europe)
Smart opened early orders at the Paris Motor Show with a starting price of 19,990 euros. Image: smart
Wolfgang Ufer, CEO of Smart Europe, said that “the time is right for the next chapter of the smart two-seater.” Smart is selling the car through its retail partners first, with online ordering following in the first half of 2027. The company notes the #2 is still going through EU homologation, so the specs could change before deliveries.
The timing makes sense. Mercedes
handed half of Smart to Geely in 2019
and turned it into a Chinese-built EV brand, but so far that has meant crossovers like the #1, #3, and the
Model Y-sized #5
. The #2 is the first car of the new era that looks like what people think of when they hear “Smart.”
The Twingo problem
The obvious rival is Renault’s new Twingo E-Tech, which also starts at €19,990 in Germany. The Twingo gets a 27.5 kWh LFP pack, up to 262 km of WLTP range, and 50 kW DC charging.
So the Smart wins on paper with 28 km more range and faster charging. But the Twingo has four seats and five doors for the same money.
And if you’re in the US, don’t get your hopes up.
Daimler pulled Smart out of the US and Canada in 2019
, and a Chinese-built car with connected services has no path into the US market under current rules.
Electrek’s Take
We like this car. The original electric Fortwo was a great idea held back by its battery. With 133 km of WLTP range and no DC fast charging, it was a city car you couldn’t take out of the city and you’d need to think twice about buying it unless you had a charging situation at home in the city. Smart never solved that after launching the
17.6 kWh Fortwo electric drive
in 2016. The #2 finally does, with twice the battery and a real fast-charging port.
But the price puts it in a tough spot. €19,990 is now the going rate for a small European EV, and at that price Renault gives you a four-seat hatchback. The two-seater’s argument has always been parking. In Paris, Rome, or Amsterdam, a car under 2.8 meters long can squeeze into spots nothing else fits, and that’s a real advantage. It’s also a niche one.
So the #2 will live or die on how many urban buyers value a tiny footprint over a back seat. The old Fortwo proved that market exists, but it was never huge. And Volkswagen’s ID. Every1 is supposed to land at around €20,000 in 2027, right when the #2 starts deliveries.
Still, this is the most compelling Smart in years. It’s a car with a clear purpose, which is more than we could say about the brand’s lineup of crossovers.

title: Huawei-backed AITO sets Europe launch for fall 2027 with 4 luxury SUVs
content:
Fred Lambert
| Oct 12 2026 - 7:48 am PT
AITO showed the AITO 9, AITO 8, AITO 7 and AITO 6 at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. Image: AITO
AITO will start selling cars in Europe in the fall of 2027. The Chinese luxury SUV brand, built by Seres with Huawei’s technology, confirmed the timing at the Paris Motor Show today, where it showed the AITO 9, 8, 7, and 6.
AITO sold 426,000 vehicles in 2025, more than any other Chinese luxury brand. Now it has a date for Europe. But you won’t find the word “Huawei” anywhere in its Paris press kit.
A year out, with a lot of paperwork left
AITO is giving itself 12 months, and it needs them. The brand says it’s still “actively pursuing” EU Whole Vehicle Type Approval, the certification any car needs to be sold in the bloc, and it’s targeting a five-star Euro NCAP rating under the 2026 protocol across its whole lineup.
Its briefing material also includes a pledge to comply with GDPR. That’s not something automakers usually feel the need to spell out, unless they expect European buyers to ask where their data goes.
The rest of the plan is localization: tuning the powertrains and chassis for European roads, multilingual voice controls in the cabin, adapting driver assistance and parking features “with partners,” and building a service network with local parts and customer support teams.
What’s missing is everything a buyer would care about. No prices. No launch markets. No dealer or distribution partners. No European specs.
And this isn’t the first time AITO has teased Europe. Seres showed the AITO 9, 8, and 5 at IAA Munich in September 2025 without giving any timeline. Seres has also been selling its own Seres 5 crossover in a couple of European markets, like Norway and Greece, for years.
Clifford Kang, Board Member and Vice President of SERES Group, announcing AITO’s plans to enter Europe in fall 2027. Image: AITO
“For AITO, New Luxury is where traditional luxury meets technological luxury,” said Clifford Kang, board member and vice president of Seres Group, during the press conference.
Big, fast, three-row SUVs
All four models are SUVs, and all of them are offered in China as both battery-electric and range-extended EVs (REEV), where a gas engine acts as a generator.
The flagship AITO 9 (sold as the M9 in China) is 5,285 mm long on a 3,125 mm wheelbase, putting it in BMW X7 and Mercedes GLS territory. AITO lists up to 497 kW (666 hp) and 0-100 km/h in 4.6 seconds, along with an 800V fully active suspension, rear-wheel steering, and a CATL battery. The five-seater is the EV version, while the six-seater uses the range extender.
At the other end, the AITO 6 is a 4,960 mm two-row SUV aimed at younger buyers. The EV version makes 340 kW and the REEV 345 kW, with 0-100 km/h in 5.2 seconds.
The company also names Bosch, CATL, Valeo, and Pirelli as suppliers, which is clearly meant to reassure European buyers.
The AITO 9 flagship SUV on display in Paris. The vehicles shown are China-spec models. Image: AITO
The Huawei-shaped hole
In China, AITO has been Huawei’s car brand in all but name. It was the first brand in Huawei’s Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance (HIMA). Huawei handled product definition, design, and sales through its own stores, and it supplied the driver-assistance system and HarmonyOS cockpit that sold the cars. Seres built them.
That arrangement wasn’t cheap. Seres reportedly paid Huawei roughly 10% per vehicle in licensing and channel fees, and its purchases from Huawei and its affiliates hit 56.05 billion yuan ($8.3 billion) in 2025.
It also just changed. On September 15, Seres took over AITO’s product definition, design, marketing, retail, and service, with Huawei moving to a support role. Two weeks later, the two companies signed a new five-year cooperation agreement.
So the Paris pitch credits the “SERES MF Platform” and unnamed “partners” instead. That makes sense for Europe, where several governments have restricted Huawei equipment in their 5G networks. AITO clearly wants buyers in Munich and Lyon to see a Seres brand, not a Huawei one.
Visitors and media at the AITO press conference at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. Image: AITO
Strong at home, but slowing
The track record in China is real. According to Seres’ annual results, AITO sold 426,000 vehicles in 2025, led by the AITO 8 (over 150,000), with the AITO 9 and AITO 7 above 110,000 each. The brand hit one million cumulative deliveries in 46 months.
But 2026 has been rougher. HIMA, where AITO is the biggest contributor, delivered 37,490 vehicles in September, down 29% year-over-year and its fourth straight monthly decline. Seres posted a 1.72 billion yuan net loss in the first half of 2026, compared with a 2.94 billion yuan profit a year earlier, as revenue fell 7.9%.
Then there’s trade policy. Chinese-built battery-electric cars face EU anti-subsidy tariffs of up to 35.3%, on top of the standard 10% import duty. Chinese automakers have
leaned on plug-in hybrids to get around them
, and AITO’s range-extended lineup would have fit right into that strategy.
That door is closing. On October 9, the EU and China agreed to halve Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid exports to the EU. Neither side has released the terms, so it’s not yet clear how range extenders will be treated.
AITO will also be late to the party. By fall 2027, it will be fighting BYD, which has already
overtaken Tesla as the best-selling EV brand in key overseas markets
, and Xpeng, which has been
in talks to buy a Volkswagen plant in Europe
, on top of the German luxury brands on their home turf.
Electrek’s Take
The AITO 9 is a genuinely impressive SUV, and Chinese buyers have spent real luxury money on it. On paper, the cabin tech and the performance match or beat what the German brands offer for the money.
The problem is that AITO’s success in China was built on Huawei. Huawei’s stores, Huawei’s software, Huawei’s brand recognition. Strip that out, and in Europe you have a big, fast, well-equipped SUV from a company almost nobody there has heard of, priced against BMW, Mercedes, and Volvo.
Chinese luxury brands have had a hard time in Europe so far. Nio has been at it for years with tiny volumes. Building a premium dealer and service network from scratch is slow and expensive, and AITO is doing it while its home sales are falling and Seres is losing money.
And the tariff picture keeps getting worse. The BEVs get hit with anti-subsidy duties, and the range-extender workaround is now being capped by an EU-China deal whose details we still don’t know.
A year out with no prices, no markets, and no partners, “autumn 2027” is a statement of intent, not a launch. We’ll take it seriously when there’s a price list and delivery dates.

title: TEMO launches clever new electric boat motor in the US
content:
Electric boats
Micah Toll
| Oct 12 2026 - 7:28 am PT
French electric marine motor manufacturer TEMO is bringing its latest electric propulsion system to North America, offering sailboat owners an interesting middle ground between a conventional outboard and a permanently installed pod drive.
It’s been nearly two years since we
last checked in on the French e-boat motor maker
, but it appears they’ve used that time well to make several new advancements, chief among them the TEMO OUTPOD system.
The novel electric boat drivetrain will make its North American debut at the United States Sailboat Show in Annapolis, Maryland, later this week. The OUTPOD was previously awarded the Best Innovative Product prize at the 2025 Paris Nautic Show, and is
now becoming available for boaters in the US
There are several electric boat motors out there, and even a few specifically designed for sailboats. But the interesting part here is how TEMO has approached installation. Traditional pod drives generally require cutting into the boat’s hull, while electric outboards hang from the transom. The OUTPOD instead places an underwater pod drive on an external, bolt-on transom mount, meaning there’s no drilling below the waterline.
The motor can also slide off its mount for storage or maintenance. A height-adjustable mast allows sailors to pull the entire motor out of the water using a halyard while sailing, eliminating the drag of leaving a propeller in the water. The shaft can rotate through 180 degrees for maneuvering and hydrogeneration.
TEMO is launching two versions. The OUTPOD 1000 produces 1,300 watts and 66 lb (30 kg) of static thrust, while the larger OUTPOD 3000 bumps that to 3,100 watts and 148 lb (67 kg) of thrust. Interestingly, the motor itself weighs just 26 lb (11.8 kg) in either version.
Power comes from removable 2.3 kWh batteries that slot into an auto-connecting rack, allowing owners to charge them either onboard using shore power or remove them for charging elsewhere. Sailors who already have a compatible 48V lithium battery bank can use that instead. It’s unclear if that only includes 48V batteries available from TEMO, but with so many
commonly available large capacity 48V batteries these days
, an open system could be quite convenient for sailors looking to add capacity or carry multiple batteries.
The system also supports both solar charging and hydrogeneration, allowing the propeller to feed energy back into the batteries while sailing.
It’s part of TEMO’s broader 48V SEASIDE ecosystem, which shares batteries and controls across several styles of electric marine motors ranging from 500W to 6kW.
The OUTPOD 1000 package starts at $2,600, while the OUTPOD·3000 carries a $5,400 MSRP. Both will be shown at the Annapolis show from October 15-18.
It’s another interesting example of how electrification can rethink marine propulsion rather than simply replacing a gasoline outboard with an electric one. For sailboats in particular, the ability to completely lift the drive out of the water when it isn’t needed – and then use it for hydrogeneration when desired – makes for a particularly compelling setup.

title: BYD reveals flagship 7-seat electric SUV with over 400 miles of range
content:
Peter Johnson
| Oct 12 2026 - 7:20 am PT
The flagship seven-seater is
first vehicle in Europe to feature its second-generation batteries and Flash Charging tech, delivering over 400 miles of range.
BYD launches new flagship Atto 8 in Europe
“BYD is all about turning intelligence into reality,” Stella Li, the company’s executive vice president, said on Monday.
The Atto 8 is the “perfect example,” Li added, featuring its latest breakthrough tech, including its second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging system.
Introduced at the Paris Auto Show, the flagship SUV is the first BYD vehicle to feature its Flash Charging system, enabling it to recharge just as fast as filling up at the gas station. It takes just five minutes to charge from 10% to 80%.
A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes. According to BYD, that’s about a third of the time rival SUVs take to go from 10% to 80%.
Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it requires only 12 minutes for the vehicle’s battery to recharge from 20% to 97%.
BYD Atto 8 at a Flash Charging station (Source: BYD)
Measuring 5,040 mm long, 1,996 mm wide, and 1,760 mm tall, the Atto 8 is about the size of other full-size electric SUVs, such as the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9.
BYD’s flagship SUV comes in two all-electric variants with the choice of rear- and all-wheel-drive powertrains.
The Design RWD model has a single rear motor producing 456 hp (340 kW) and 269 lb-ft (365 Nm) of torque, which BYD said delivers a 0 to 62 mph time of eight seconds.
BYD Atto 8 (Source: BYD)
Powered by a 115 kWh BYD Blade 2.0 battery, the Atto 8 offers an impressive WLTP range of up to 405 miles (600+ km). For example, BYD said the flagship SUV offers enough electric range to drive from London to Edinburgh.
The Atto 8 Excellence AWD, on the other hand, adds a front electric motor for a combined output of 764 hp (570 kW) and 572 lb-ft (775 Nm) of torque. The added power delivers a sports-car-rivaling 0- 62 mph acceleration time of 4.6 seconds and a WLTP range of 374 miles.
BYD Atto 8 interior (Source: BYD)
Inside, natural light fills the spacious cabin thanks to a 2.39m2 panoramic glass roof. Both Atto 8 variants have a 10.25″ digital instrument cluster, a 26″ head-up display, and a 15.6″ central infotainment touchscreen with Google Built-in.
BYD said the Atto 8 is specifically tailored for those looking for a “zero compromise” seven-seat SUV.
The front seats and outer seats of the middle row feature heating, ventilation, and massage functions. Rear passengers get their own air-conditioning control panel. All seats are upholstered in genuine leather.
The Design RWD model features a 10-speaker sound system, while the Excellence AWD gains a 21-speaker DiSound audio system, plus an added front refrigerator.
With the second and third rows folded, the Atto 8 offers up to 1,960L capacity. Even with all three rows up, the full-size SUV offers 270L of luggage space. Plus, there’s a 136L frunk (front trunk).
BYD said dealers in Europe will begin selling the Atto 8 in the first quarter of 2027. Prices have yet to be announced, but given it will be positioned above
the Ti 7
, a plug-in hybrid seven-seat SUV, it will likely start at slightly over £47,995 ($65,000) on the road in the UK.
In Europe, BYD currently sells the Tang, an electric seven-seat SUV. In Germany, the
BYD Tang
typically starts at €75,000 ($84,000), but it’s currently on sale for €47,990 ($54,000).

title: NHTSA weighs probe into claims Tesla Robotaxis speed in school zones
content:
Tesla Autopilot
Fred Lambert
| Oct 12 2026 - 6:24 am PT
A new defect petition accuses Tesla’s Robotaxis of speeding through active school zones, and NHTSA has opened a file to decide whether to investigate. The agency puts the affected fleet at about 1,000 vehicles, Model Y and Cybercab.
It’s the third federal action aimed at Tesla’s driverless fleet in about five weeks, after an audit query and a Special Order over how the Cybercab was certified.
A petition, not an investigation (yet)
The Office of Defects Investigation opened the file, DP26010, on Friday, October 9, according to the agency’s
opening resume
. The request itself reached NHTSA on September 23 and targets model year 2026 Robotaxis running with Tesla’s Automated Driving System (ADS) engaged.
The evidence file is small: three social media videos, linked in the petition, and four incidents in NHTSA’s own tally. No crashes, injuries, or deaths.
Federal rules (49 CFR Part 552) give NHTSA 120 days from receiving a petition to grant or deny it, which puts the deadline around January 21, 2027. A grant means a formal defect investigation, and those can end in a recall.
NHTSA just put a number on Tesla’s fleet
The 1,000 figure is news on its own. Tesla doesn’t disclose how many Robotaxis it operates, and as recently as June, community trackers counted only a few dozen active cars across Austin, Dallas, and Houston, as
we reported at the time
Tesla has added the Cybercab since, starting commercial service in Austin on September 3. NHTSA labels its count an estimate. Still, it’s the first federal number we’ve seen for the size of the fleet.
It appears that NHTSA might be using the number of vehicles Tesla is officially adding to the fleet through the Texas DMV certification, but those are not all active in the fleet.
Speed has come up before
This isn’t the first time Tesla’s software has been flagged for speed. Videos from the Austin Robotaxi launch in June 2025 showed cars going over the limit, and NHTSA said at the time it was in contact with Tesla about them.
In October 2025, NHTSA opened
another investigation into Full Self-Driving
over traffic-law violations like running red lights and driving into the wrong lane. A week later, Tesla shipped a
“Mad Max” FSD profile that ignores speed limits
But there’s an important difference here. With FSD (Supervised), the owner picks a profile and is responsible for the car. A Robotaxi has no owner behind the wheel. When the ADS decides how fast to go past a school, Tesla made that decision.
The petition lands on top of the Cybercab certification fight. NHTSA
ordered Tesla to prove under oath
that a car with no pedals or steering wheel meets federal safety standards, with answers due September 30. NHTSA hasn’t made Tesla’s answers public.
Waymo had its own school problem
Waymo isn’t clean here either. Late last year, Austin ISD reported Waymo vehicles illegally passing stopped school buses about 20 times, and Waymo answered with a voluntary software recall in December 2025. We
covered the fallout
when Waymo’s founder went after Tesla’s safety record in the middle of it.
Waymo fixed it with a recall filed with NHTSA. We’ll see if Tesla does the same, or waits for the agency to decide for it.
Whatever happens with this petition, the cheapest way to power an EV is still the sun on your own roof. title: Electric trucks meet hydro power at one of Canada's busiest ports
content:
Commercial EVs
electric trucks
Jo Borrás
| Oct 12 2026 - 6:18 am PT
Electric work trucks are earning their keep at one of Canada’s busiest container terminals, where Peterbilt’s battery-powered box vans are keeping cargo moving without the air pollution of diesel and propane. And now, they’re getting recognized for it.
“Sustainability in action. We’re thrilled to congratulate our partners at GCT for winning the BC Hydro Luminaries Project of the Year,” reads the official Peterbilt copy. “Seeing our Peterbilt 520EV fuel tankers and 220EV lubrication trucks powering the largest fleet rollout of any terminal in Canada is a true testament to the hard work of everyone involved.”
Port of Vancouver
terminal operator GCT has committed to reducing its absolute emissions by 45% by 2030 and reaching true net zero by 2050 across both its Vanterm and Deltaport terminals. As part of that effort, GCT is rolling out a fleet of electric equipment assets that includes two electric Peterbilts – a 220EV lubrication service truck that maintains the terminal’s rubber-tired gantry cranes and a 520EV tanker that refuels older, diesel-powered equipment still sprinkled around the company’s terminals.
For their parts, Peterbilt executives seem to like getting awards and being called luminaries. “This is a perfect example of electrification innovation,” wrote Peterbilt national sales manager, Martin Blanchet,
on LinkedIn
. “Zero-Emission vehicles operating on port premises typically have high idle ratios and significant ePTO requirements, making them an ideal fit for Peterbilt’s electric vocational trucks. Congratulations to GCT Global Container Terminals and Peterbilt Pacific on this great deployment.”
The trucks, themselves
Model 520EV at Port of Vancouver; via Peterbilt.
A quick perusal of Peterbilt’s website indicates that the trucks themselves are standard
Peterbilt
offerings that have been upfit for their particular vocations. The 220EV is offered with up to 282 kWh of battery capacity and up to 259 kW (~345 hp) of continuous power, while the heavier duty 520EV packs 400 kWh and puts out 400 kW (~535 hp). Both trucks do their jobs without tailpipe emissions, of course, dramatically reducing the air pollution typically associated with conventional, diesel-powered trucks AND
saving GCT big money
These trucks join the fleet of electric Peterbilt 579EV Class 8 trucks that’s already being put to work on container-hauling routes at the Port of Vancouver as part of a new
, data-sharing pilot program designed to measure real-world benefits of electric drayage trucks on first-mile delivery routes. Funded through Canada’s ELECTRA (ELEctric Container TRucking progrAm), the new pilot is working with five port shipping companies, providing heavily subsidized 60-month lease terms on new Class 8 electric semi trucks and their supporting charging infrastructure.

title: This electric motorcycle company just hit 10 million battery swaps – and it’s profitable
content:
Electric Motorcycles
battery swap
Micah Toll
| Oct 12 2026 - 4:30 am PT
Brazilian electric motorcycle and battery-swapping company Vammo is hitting several major milestones as it prepares to take its model beyond its home of São Paulo, including reaching EBITDA profitability, surpassing 10 million battery swaps, and growing to more than 10,000 active riders.
Vammo has operated in São Paulo since 2022, building out a network that
now includes
roughly 1,000 battery-swapping points. Riders use the company’s electric motorcycles and can pull into a swapping location to exchange depleted batteries for charged packs rather than waiting around to plug in.
Early last year, we covered the company’s major milestone of
reaching 1 million battery swaps
. Now Vammo is adding another zero to that number.
co-founder and Chief Operating Officer explained to
Electrek
how the company is beginning its first significant geographic expansion, with Campinas set to become its second official city. Vammo plans to remain focused on the broader state of São Paulo for now before eventually expanding throughout Brazil and into other Latin American markets, cruising towards becoming the Gogoro of Latin America.
That pace might sound like a relatively conservative expansion plan, but remember that São Paulo alone represents a massive two-wheeler market. In just that one state, more than 500,000 motorcycles are sold annually – or more than the entire US motorcycle market.
And the company’s existing operating territory is already huge. Vammo says its current service area around São Paulo is geographically comparable to the San Francisco Bay Area and contains around 26 million people.
The company has now performed more than 10 million battery swaps and expects that figure to exceed 100 million sometime in 2027. Active customers have increased 250% this year alone to more than 10,000, while Vammo says it is on track to reach around $45 million in annual recurring revenue by the end of 2026.
Perhaps more importantly for a capital-intensive business involving both vehicles and physical infrastructure, Vammo says it reached breakeven in June – six months earlier than planned – and is now comfortably EBITDA profitable.
That’s a rarity
among young electric motorcycle companies.
The company is also rolling out its third-generation swapping station, which it says reduces costs by another 15%. The new stations use AI-based software to dynamically adjust battery charging rates based on factors including real-time and predicted rider demand, weather, delivery-app demand, customer usage patterns, and battery temperature.
There’s still a huge amount of room for electric motorcycles to grow in Brazil.
Vammo says data from Brazilian vehicle industry association FENABRAVE shows 11,587 electric motorcycles were registered from January through August this year, an 85% increase year-over-year. Yet electric models still account for just 0.7% of motorcycle sales, a veritable drop in the bucket.
But among that small yet growing slice of the pie, Vammo reigns supreme. The company claims more than 65% of Brazil’s electric motorcycle market so far this year, and if its growth continues at the current rate, we could see that share balloon even further.
That’s particularly interesting in a country where motorcycles play a much larger transportation role than they do in North America, especially for delivery and other commercial riders. Brazil also generates the large majority of its electricity from renewable sources, particularly hydropower, with rapidly growing wind and solar generation. That means electrifying motorcycles there can offer an unusually compelling combination: replacing gasoline-powered transportation with electric vehicles that are themselves charged largely from low-carbon electricity.
And there’s a strong economic argument for riders, too. Vammo says its average customer saves around 35% compared to operating the typical alternative, a used 160cc gasoline motorcycle. Much of those savings comes from lower energy and maintenance costs – two key wins for electric motorbikes.
The company has also launched a new 36-month rent-to-own program aimed at tackling another distinctly Brazilian problem: expensive vehicle financing, where Vammo says rates can approach 45%. At the end of the rental period, riders can purchase the motorcycle for the same amount they originally put down as a deposit. They can then either purchase a battery or continue using Vammo’s swapping network.
Battery swapping has been tried in plenty of markets, often with mixed results. But two-wheelers remain perhaps the strongest use case for the technology. Their batteries are small enough to physically swap by hand, commercial riders can’t afford hours of charging downtime, and dense urban usage makes a swapping network easier to support.
With 10 million swaps already under its belt, profitability achieved, and its first expansion beyond São Paulo underway, Vammo is starting to demonstrate what that model looks like at serious scale.
And considering electric motorcycles still make up less than 1% of Brazil’s motorcycle market, the company may still be writing just the first chapter of that story.

The French Energy Regulatory Commission (CRE) has proposed an initial framework for implementing the country’s new capacity mechanism ahead of the first long-term auction, covering the winter of 2030-31.
The mechanism is designed to reduce the risk of electricity supply shortages during periods of system stress, particularly at times of peak demand. It compensates operators of generation, storage and demand-response assets for committing to make their capacity available during critical periods.
Once fully implemented, the new mechanism will rely on two complementary auctions: a long-term auction held approximately four years before the delivery period and a short-term auction held around one year in advance. The first short-term auction took place on July 6, 2026, for the winter of 2026-27.
Based on a report submitted by French transmission system operator RTE following extensive stakeholder consultations, CRE has proposed a methodology to the French energy minister for determining the demand curve and the technical and economic parameters for the first long-term auction, covering the winter of 2030-31.
New capacity needs estimated at up to 2.5 GW
The auction comes during the transition from France’s previous capacity mechanism to the new system. Under the current timetable, market participants will have to make commitments for the winter of 2030-31 before securing capacity contracts for the three preceding winters, from 2027-28 to 2029-30.
This creates uncertainty for investment and contracting strategies. However, RTE’s analysis suggests that risks to security of supply remain moderate, with additional capacity requirements estimated at between 0 GW and 2.5 GW, depending on the scenario.
Against this backdrop, CRE has opted for a cautious approach to setting the economic parameters to limit costs for consumers. The regulator said the approach could evolve in future auctions as market participants gain experience with the mechanism and CRE and RTE assess the results.
Auction to target 82 GW of capacity
For the first long-term auction, CRE has proposed a target volume of 82 GW, including 3 GW eligible for multi-year contracts. According to the regulator, the proposed volume is consistent with France’s security-of-supply objectives, electrification plans and expected growth in electricity demand.
CRE has also proposed certification parameters intended to support the development of different capacity technologies. Particular attention has been given to battery storage, which is expected to play an increasingly important role in providing flexibility and balancing services to the electricity system.
On pricing, CRE has proposed maintaining the mechanism’s two price caps, known as PPG and PPI, at €72 ($80.4)/kW and €15/kW, respectively. The regulator said the caps are intended to contain costs for consumers while allowing different capacity technologies to recover their costs.
CRE also plans to continue refining the methodology for future auctions, taking into account the initial results of the new mechanism and feedback from market participants.

content:

South African utility Eskom has launched a qualification process to select strategic partners for up to 6 GW of renewable energy and storage projects. The portfolio will include at least 2 GW of solar and 1 GW/4 GWh of battery storage, with selected developers joining a five-year co-development and investment framework.
Emiliano Bellini
12 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Eskom’s thermal power plant in the Mpumalanga province
South Africa’s state-owned power utility
has launched a
request for qualification (RFQ)
process to select renewable energy developers for the first phase of a program aimed at deploying up to 6 GW of utility-scale renewable energy and energy storage projects.
“The Eskom Phase 1 Programme is an initial portfolio of up to 6 GW of utility-scale renewable energy projects, spanning solar photovoltaic (PV), battery energy storage systems (BESS), wind and other renewable technologies,” the company said in a statement. “Eskom will contribute projects comprising at least 2GW of solar PV and 1GW / 4GWh of BESS, which may be complemented by projects owned or originated by the selected strategic partners. The strategic partners will form a panel of pre-qualified co-development and co-investment partners for development, financing and implementation for a period of five years.”
Qualified developers will be invited to participate in subsequent competitive procurement rounds through one or more requests for proposals (RFPs).
The planned portfolio includes Eskom-originated projects on utility-owned land and at existing generation sites, alongside projects owned or originated by strategic partners that could be developed, acquired or implemented in partnership with Eskom or its Eskom Green subsidiary.
Each project is expected to be structured through a dedicated, ring-fenced special purpose vehicle (SPV), with financing primarily arranged on a limited-recourse or non-recourse project finance basis.
Eskom launched Eskom Green in July
as part of its broader restructuring strategy, which includes the
unbundling process initiated in 2023
Despite these developments, Eskom remains under financial pressure. The utility continues to rely on coal-fired generation and diesel-fired peaking plants. Diesel expenditure remains in the hundreds of millions of South African rand, although it has declined significantly from the previous year.
Meanwhile, South Africa is advancing electricity market reforms, including plans to establish a wholesale electricity market that could reshape Eskom’s role in the power sector. Analysts have warned that regulatory provisions favoring Eskom’s coal-fired assets could discourage private investment and undermine efficiency gains, potentially increasing long-term electricity costs for consumers.

title: Multiple grounding points cut lightning-induced overvoltage in solar panels by up to 55% - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in Indonesia found that higher soil resistivity significantly increases lightning-induced overvoltage in PV systems. Their simulations also showed that multiple grounding points and connections closer to the lightning strike location can substantially reduce transient voltages.
Emiliano Bellini
12 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Utility-scale
A research team in Indonesia has proposed a novel grounding strategy to mitigate lightning-induced overvoltage in PV systems by identifying optimal grounding-point locations and evaluating different grounding configurations.
“Previous research has generally protected solar panels using a Lightning Protection System (LPS) with lightning rods connected to down conductors, such as Franklin rods,” the scientists emphasized. “This study considers the possibility of direct lightning strikes on solar panels or their supports, even if an LPS is installed. This occurrence allows current to flow through the solar panels to the grounding point.”
The researchers developed an equivalent electrical circuit model to investigate the transient overvoltage response of PV systems to lightning strikes. The simulated array comprised ten solar panels, each rated at 200 W, representing a section of a larger PV installation. Using ATPDraw 7.2 software, they modeled the electrical characteristics of the PV frames, mounting structures, grounding conductors, and electrodes through equivalent resistance, inductance, capacitance, and mutual inductance parameters.
Lightning strikes were simulated using a Heidler current source with a peak amplitude of 50 kA and an impulse waveform of 1.2/50 μs. Two configurations were investigated: direct grounding through the PV module frames and grounding through the mounting structures. The simulations assessed the effects of soil resistivity, grounding-point location, and the number of grounding connections on transient voltage distribution.
The researchers varied grounding-point locations to determine how the electrical path between the lightning strike location and the grounding connection influences overvoltage levels. They also compared single- and dual-grounding arrangements to assess the benefits of additional connections. The model assumed electrically interconnected metallic PV frames and evaluated voltage differences relative to a reference potential, excluding physical damage mechanisms and potential differences involving PV power conductors and inverters.
The results showed that increasing soil resistivity from 30 Ωm to 3,000 Ωm significantly raised transient voltage levels in both configurations. At lower resistivities, the highest voltages occurred near the lightning injection point, whereas at 3,000 Ωm, they shifted toward the grounding connection. Grounding through the mounting structures generally resulted in lower maximum voltages due to their lower electrical resistance.
At a constant soil resistivity of 30 Ωm, maximum voltages ranged from 1.97 MV to 2.64 MV for frame grounding and from 2.14 MV to 2.43 MV for mounting-based grounding, depending on the connection location. In both cases, positioning the grounding point closest to the lightning injection point minimized peak voltages by shortening the current discharge path and reducing its impedance.
Introducing a second grounding point further reduced transient voltages by 47.5% to 54.8% for frame grounding and by 43.2% to 50.7% for mounting-based grounding. The researchers attributed these improvements to lower grounding impedance and more efficient lightning current dissipation. The simulated peak current reached 48.78 kA, which the researchers described as being within the safety limits of IEEE Std 80, the IEEE Guide for Safety in AC Substation Grounding.
The findings indicate that grounding-point location and the number of connections have a greater influence on transient voltage mitigation than the choice between frame- and mounting-based grounding. In particular, shorter discharge paths, lower grounding resistance, and multiple grounding connections can substantially improve grounding performance.
Overall, the study highlights the importance of strategically positioned grounding points, low-resistivity soil conditions, and multipoint grounding in reducing lightning-induced overvoltage and improving the reliability of PV installations.
The new methodology was presented in “
Study of the selection of an individual grounding location point against direct lightning strikes on solar panel systems
,” published in
Results in Engineering
. The research group comprised scientists from Indonesia’s Institut Teknologi Sepuluh Nopember and Universitas Hasanuddin.

title: Energy Dome opens CO2 battery manufacturing plant in Italy - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Energy Dome’s new manufacturing plant will supply components for long-duration energy storage (LDES) projects in India, the United States and Ireland.
Sergio Matalucci
12 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Italian long-duration energy storage (LDES) company Energy Dome has opened a manufacturing plant in Piacenza, Italy, as it expands production of its CO2 Battery technology for international projects.
The facility will manufacture key components, including the large domes used in the company’s carbon dioxide-based energy storage systems.
Energy Dome said it has shipped the first dome manufactured entirely in-house to India for the 20 MW/160 MWh Kudgi project with state-owned power company NTPC. Production is underway for the 20 MW/200 MWh Columbia Energy Storage Project in Wisconsin, United States, with Alliant Energy. The next component is destined for a 23 MW/200 MWh project in Rhode, Ireland.
The company invested approximately €2 million ($2.2 million) in the Piacenza site over the past year to upgrade the building, acquire machinery and improve electrical and network infrastructure. It plans to increase total investment to approximately €6.5 million over the next two years, with the goal of tripling production capacity and expanding the local workforce from 30 employees to between 80 and 90 by 2028.
Energy Dome said its technology relies on European manufacturing supply chains, including steel and turbomachinery, rather than supply chains located outside Europe.
The company reports a presence across four continents, with more than 2 GWh of projects operational or under contract, more than 3 GWh of authorized projects and a development pipeline exceeding 30 GWh. Its customers and partners include Google, Engie, Alliant Energy, NTPC, SEC and SRP.
Energy Dome also cited Italy’s National Integrated Energy and Climate Plan, grid operator Terna’s stated need for 50 GWh of storage by 2030 and the new MACSE storage procurement mechanism as factors supporting demand for energy storage.

title: Study identifies new PID degradation mechanism in medium-voltage PV modules - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
French researchers have found that increasing PV system voltage significantly worsens potential-induced degradation (PID), with encapsulant conductivity playing a key role in module performance. They also identified a new degradation mechanism involving partial discharges and electrical treeing, highlighting additional reliability risks for medium-voltage PV modules.
Emiliano Bellini
12 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
EVA encapsulant
Researchers at the
research institute of the
French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission
(CEA) have investigated how increasing PV system voltage affects
potential-induced degradation
(PID) in solar modules, focusing on the relationship between encapsulant electrical conductivity and module performance.
The scientists said this is the first study to investigate PID in passivated emitter and rear cell (PERC) solar modules at voltages as high as 6,000 V and to identify partial-discharge-induced electrical treeing as an additional degradation mechanism in medium-voltage PV modules. “PERC modules were chosen even though they are progressively being phased out; this cell technology has been well studied and is therefore a logical choice for investigating medium-voltage degradation phenomena,” they explained.
Their analysis considered four encapsulant materials – ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA), polyolefin elastomer (POE), thermoplastic polyolefin (TPO), and ionomer – under controlled electric field, temperature, and humidity conditions. For the tests, they used 20 cm × 20 cm glass-glass PV mini-modules, each containing a half-cut bifacial PERC cell.
Conductivity was measured using a parallel-plate electrode configuration with gold-coated polymer samples, applying voltages of up to 3,000 V through alternating two-hour polarization and depolarization cycles. The researchers conducted two experimental campaigns. The first examined PID at 1,500 V, 3,000 V, and 6,000 V using nine TPO-based modules, while the second compared the PID resistance of the four encapsulants at 3,000 V. All modules underwent accelerated aging for 96 hours at 85 C and 85% relative humidity.
Current-voltage (I-V) measurements under standard test conditions were performed before and after aging to quantify electrical performance losses on both sides of the bifacial modules. Electroluminescence (EL), photoluminescence (PL), and external quantum efficiency (EQE) measurements were used to characterize degradation mechanisms.
The analysis showed that encapsulant electrical conductivity strongly depends on electric field and temperature, significantly influencing PID. For example, TPO conductivity increased with applied voltage, while raising the temperature from approximately 20 C to 80 C increased conductivity by two orders of magnitude. Further PID testing revealed progressively greater power losses with increasing voltage magnitude, particularly on the rear side of the modules. At 6,000 V, maximum power losses reached 13.5% on the front side and 19.5% on the rear side.
The researchers also found that front-side degradation was primarily associated with sodium-ion migration, while rear-side degradation was mainly attributed to charge accumulation and polarization. Following testing at 6,000 V, rear-side power losses increased to 26% during dark storage but fell to 9.8% after illumination, indicating partial recovery.
A comparison of the four encapsulants at 3,000 V revealed a strong correlation between electrical conductivity and degradation severity. TPO exhibited the highest rear-side power loss at 23.6%, followed by EVA at 21.7%, ionomer at 13.0%, and POE at 4.6%. Power losses increased approximately linearly with the logarithm of conductivity, at rates of 1.8 and 4.9 percentage points per tenfold increase in conductivity on the front and rear sides, respectively.
POE demonstrated the greatest resistance to PID, although residual fill-factor losses suggested possible metallization-related degradation. EL and PL imaging confirmed the electrical performance trends. The researchers also observed partial-discharge-induced electrical treeing exclusively in ionomer-based modules at 3,000 V, particularly near metallic cell ribbons and glass-encapsulant interfaces. They identified this phenomenon as a new PID degradation mechanism, referred to as PID-discharge (PID-d).
The authors attributed this phenomenon to locally enhanced electric fields associated with reduced encapsulant thickness, ribbon geometry, and possible insulation weaknesses. The discharges appeared to cause localized cavities and delamination, potentially compromising long-term electrical insulation.
Overall, the findings highlight the importance of low-conductivity encapsulants, adequate insulation thickness, and optimized module design for mitigating PID and partial-discharge risks in medium-voltage PV systems. “This study demonstrates that moving toward higher system voltages is not without risks for PV modules; however, these risks can already be effectively quantified and identified through appropriate laboratory testing and material qualification,” the researchers concluded.
Their findings are presented in the study “
Degradation of photovoltaic modules at medium voltage with different types of encapsulants
,” published in
Solar Energy

title: South Korea details auction market to replace renewable quota system - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Draft rules for South Korea’s new renewables auction market provide for monthly difference payments from Korea Electric Power Corp. (Kepco), a separate track for projects up to 500 kW, and an exit route for renewable energy certificate (REC) spot-market sellers.
Brian Publicover
12 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Renewable Energy Certificates
Utility-scale
South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment has published draft implementing rules for the auction-based “contract market” that will replace the country’s renewable quota system from Jan. 1, 2027. It presented them at a public hearing in Seoul on Sept. 30.
Under the draft enforcement decree, Kepco will sign long-term fixed-price contracts with winning projects on behalf of all entities required to buy the power, including local electricity suppliers and large consumers that purchase directly from the market. It will settle the difference between the contract price and the wholesale power price with each project monthly and recover the costs through electricity tariffs.
The ministry plans to hold two to four tenders a year, organized by energy source, with total auction volumes rising year on year under five-year roadmaps. A solar and onshore wind roadmap is due by the end of the year, aligned with the 12th Basic Plan for Electricity Supply and Demand. The offshore wind roadmap was published in June. A public-private cost evaluation committee will set ceiling prices for each energy source annually, at a level reflecting generation costs plus a reasonable return.
Bids will be scored on price and on non-price factors, which the draft enforcement rule lists as community acceptance, contribution to the domestic renewables industry, and grid impact. The REC multipliers used under the current system will be converted into “preferential prices.” The ministry’s examples include floating, agrivoltaic, and rooftop solar, projects in areas with spare grid capacity, community ownership, and contributions to supply chains and energy security.
Projects of 500 kW or less will compete in a separate contract market under the same ceiling prices. Portfolios of at least 1 MW aggregated as virtual power plants could receive incentives for bidding into the main market, and designated renewable energy service companies will support small developers.
Large public generators, defined as those with at least 500 MW of conventional or 100 MW of renewable capacity, will face capacity-based deployment obligations. They can meet these only by building projects directly or taking equity stakes, and face penalties of up to 150% of a government-set unit price for shortfalls.
Private generators with at least 500 MW and selected public institutions will instead be set deployment targets, with fines of KRW 10 million ($7,500) for missing them. The ministry is also considering reflecting compliance in environmental, social, and governance ratings. Up to 20% of an obligation or target can be met through an alternative compliance payment, rising to 30% for the first three years.
New projects will stop receiving RECs after Dec. 31, 2026, while existing projects keep issuing them for up to 20 years. The REC spot market will close at the end of 2029. Before then, spot-market sellers can bid into an annual “transition market” for long-term contracts covering the rest of their 20-year term, with ceiling prices falling each year to encourage early switching. Total quota obligations will be frozen at 2026 levels.
A new type of generation information certificate will replace RECs as the attribute-tracking instrument. For projects in the contract market, the certificates will pass to KEPCO for use in its green premium program. Other projects can sell theirs to corporate RE100 buyers through a Korea Energy Agency platform.
The ministry plans to publish a detailed implementation plan in November, finalize the regulations by the end of 2026, and announce the first contract-market tender in the first quarter of 2027. It said all figures in the drafts could change after consultation.
The amended law was
promulgated
on Sept. 15. About 210,000 plants with a combined 35.4 GW were registered under the quota system as of September, according to written remarks to the hearing by Kim Jung-ho, chair of the National Assembly’s Climate, Energy, Environment and Labor Committee.
The last solar tender under the outgoing system,
launched in July
, sought about 1 GW at a ceiling price of KRW 147,686/MWh and added premiums of up to KRW 16,000/MWh for projects using low-carbon modules. That’s an early version of the preferential prices planned for the contract market.
Battery storage remains outside the new scheme and is procured through a separate
central contract market
run by the Korea Power Exchange. The ministry has also begun funding
storage on congested distribution lines
in the Honam and Jeju regions to connect queued solar projects.

title: Risen releases 23.5%-efficient anti-glare heterojunction solar module - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Risen Energy has unveiled a new anti-glare heterojunction solar module featuring a dual-layer optical design and a power output of up to 730 W. The bifacial panel achieves a maximum efficiency of 23.5% and has received Class AAA anti-glare certification from TÜV Rheinland.
Emiliano Bellini
12 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
The Hyper-ion anti-glare HJT module
Chinese solar module manufacturer
Risen Energy
has unveiled a new heterojunction (HJT) solar module featuring a dual-layer optical design to reduce glare.
The company said the new product is part of its Hyper-ion series and is designed for installations with stringent glare-control requirements, such as those near airports and residential areas, where reflected sunlight may cause visual disturbances.
“Risen Energy’s capabilities in photovoltaic optical safety extend beyond product development. It is also the principal drafting organization behind T/CPIA0119-2025, the group standard for Photovoltaic Module Glare Testing Method,” the manufacturer said in a statement. “The launch of Hyper-ion anti-glare module represents the translation of this accumulated technical and standardization expertise into a commercial product.”
According to Risen Energy, the module uses a dual-layer optical design combining a micron-scale matte glass surface, produced through a process it calls “nanocrystalline phase reconstruction,” with technology to suppress internal reflections. The company did not provide further technical details about the process.
The manufacturer said tests conducted by Germany’s TÜV Rheinland showed a maximum daylight glare probability (DGP) of 0.30, below the Class AAA threshold of 0.35, and a maximum glare luminance of 3,463.94 cd/m², compared with a limit of 20,000 cd/m². The module also achieved a specular reflectance as low as 0.85%, according to the company.
The RSM132-8-710-730BHDG module comes in five versions, with power outputs of 710 W, 715 W, 720 W, 725 W and 730 W. Their conversion efficiencies range from 22.9% to 23.5%, while open-circuit voltages range from 50.01 V to 50.33 V and short-circuit currents from 18.00 A to 18.38 A.
The bifacial module features 132 HJT cells and measures 2,384 mm × 1,303 mm × 33 mm. It weighs 37.5 kg and features 2 mm anti-glare glass on the front and 2 mm heat-strengthened glass on the rear, along with an anodized aluminum alloy frame.
Under bifacial nameplate irradiance conditions, with rear-side irradiance of 135 W/m², the module delivers between 796 W and 818 W, according to the manufacturer’s specifications. With a 10% rear-side power gain, its equivalent power output ranges from 781 W to 803 W.
The panel has a temperature coefficient of -0.24%/C for maximum power, an operating temperature range of -40 C to 70 C, and a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V. It can withstand mechanical test loads of up to 5,400 Pa on the front and 2,400 Pa on the rear, depending on the installation method.
Risen Energy offers a 15-year product warranty and a 30-year linear power output warranty. The company specifies an annual degradation rate of 0.3% over 30 years, with guaranteed power output of 90.3% at the end of the warranty period.

title: C&I storage the ‘sleeping giant waking up’, says WoodMac - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Global energy storage outlook will see a seven-fold growth by 2035 passing 7 TWh, with falling costs and policy support accelerating battery storage momentum in emerging and advancing markets
Anna Darmani
12 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
The global energy storage market is entering a new phase of scale and complexity, according to Wood Mackenzie’s latest outlook. Cumulative capacity is forecast to grow to more than 7 TWh by 2035. Demand growth in 2026 alone is close to 30%.
But growth at that rate and capacity is no longer the most interesting part of the story. The composition is.
Global energy storage outlook by segment (% of total MWh installed in 2026)
Regional competition: the running order is changing faster than the totals suggest
While China and the United States (US) are still the two biggest global energy storage markets, in 2026, for the first time, Europe’s annual installation overtook annual US energy storage capacity and took second place after China.
In the utility segment, government-led tenders remain the main market drivers, having globally cleared over 80 GW (de-rated) capacity, with India the single largest contributor. Poland has become the global number-one emerging market, on the back of capacity-market auctions and a grid short of flexibility.
In mature utility markets, the demand signals behind the forecast are also firm. Contracted offtake for storage has passed 130 GW, with utility power purchase agreements and tolling deals together accounting for more than three-quarters of all contracts signed, according to our global offtake tracker.
In the residential landscape, the centre of gravity has shifted south: Australia has overtaken Germany as the world’s leading residential energy storage market, with more than half a million installations under its Cheaper Home Batteries subsidy, while the US market contracts this year as tax credits become less available.
Commercial and industrial storage is the sleeping giant now waking
Wood Mackenzie forecasts commercial and industrial storage capacity separately. The split shows industrial demand is materially larger in some regions.
A single “utility” line no longer tells the story: standalone still leads, but some regions need pairing far more than others
In the latest market outlook update, Wood Mackenzie changes how the utility energy storage market is measured. The utility segment is now reported in three parts: standalone, solar-paired and wind-paired, instead of one, because the three are growing for different reasons, at different speeds and in different places.
Standalone projects still dominate and will keep doing so through 2035. But paired capacity is no longer a rounding error: close to a third of the storage expected online by 2035 will sit alongside a wind or solar plant.
The new breakdown exposes how little the regions resemble one another, given their different policy and economic parameters.
Europe is the most standalone-heavy market in the world, with the overwhelming majority of its utility pipeline unpaired. Yet it is also poised for the fastest growth in paired capacity, as worsening economics for standalone solar push developers towards co-location. That makes Europe the market most likely to shift quickly towards co-location as an economic solution for stranded solar projects in markets such as Spain or Germany.
The Americas sit at the opposite end, where, for example, in the US, close to half of utility storage additions are solar-paired — a legacy of the ITC pairing requirement in the early days and now poor solar capture rates in key markets like CAISO. That share is expected to fall as storage spreads into lower solar-penetration states, where standalone economics work better.
Data centre-linked battery projects are also taking shape in the US, though not all of them are paired with wind or solar: gas-plus-storage pairings are the new co-location favorites for emerging data center projects.
Asia Pacific sits in between, with solar pairing the fastest-growing utility category, driven largely by India, which has overtaken Australia as the region’s largest utility-scale market. Regulatory changes are central to this: India’s new rules will require solar and wind projects commissioned after July 2027 to include co-located storage equal to at least 10% of capacity, rising to a four-hour minimum duration from 2029.
The replacement cycle and repowering appear in the energy storage market at last
Aging storage assets will only start to come offline and be replaced at scale after 2030, adding 40 GWh of repowered capacity by 2035, led by the US, Japan and Germany. This is the first sign of a market old enough to need replacing, which has earned a reporting line in our latest energy storage outlook.
Wood Mackenzie is hosting a global energy storage outlook webinar on 3 November to discuss which
markets and segments are shaping the future of global energy storage.
Anna Darmani
is a research director on the Wood Mackenzie Power & Renewables team, heading the EMEA energy storage team. She previously worked at EIT InnoEnergy, developing innovation and technology roadmaps and contributing to EU research and advisory projects.
