title: Anker Solix announces wheeled power station with 4.5 kW output - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The wheeled unit weighs 44 kg, with dual-voltage output and claimed idle consumption below 9 W in 120 V mode.
Tristan Rayner
12 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Energy Storage
Residential
Anker Solix has announced its S5000 portable power station, offering 5,024 Wh of storage and 4.5 kW of rated output. The lithium iron phosphate (LFP) system supports both 120 V and 240 V appliances, with battery capacity expandable to 30 kWh.
At 44 kg, or approximately 97 lb, the S5000 puts some pressure on the portable part of the description. It has wheels and a telescoping handle, which should help on level ground. Getting it up stairs or into a vehicle is another matter, and something we’ll look at in a forthcoming review.
The S5000 portable power station or solar generator as they’re known is a larger counterpart to the Anker Solix
S2000 reviewed by
ESS News
earlier this year
. The new model offers 5,024 Wh of storage and 4.5 kW of rated output, up from approximately 2 kWh and 1.5 kW on the smaller unit. Power demands are hardly decreasing and bigger unit sizes and options are key for brands exploring where demand centers.
Like the S2000, the S5000 uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, with Anker emphasizing low idle consumption and claiming up to 10,000 charge cycles. The S5000 adds dual 120 V/240 V output, battery expansion to 30 kWh, and up to 3 kW of solar input, compared with the S2000’s 400 W.
As with the
C2000 Gen 2
, announced around this time in 2025, Anker is emphasizing reduced idle power consumption. The S5000 is specified at 8.8 W draw in 120 V mode, rising to 13.7 W at 240 V. The company brands this as OptiSave 2.0 and claims longer runtime under light loads, where the power station’s own consumption can account for a larger share of battery use.
The US model has four standard NEMA 5-20 AC outlets, a TT-30 RV outlet, and an L14-30 outlet for 240 V loads. USB connections include one 100 W USB-C port, a second rated at 15 W, and a 12 W USB-A port.
Solar input is rated at up to 3 kW across two inputs. Anker specifies a full recharge in 99 minutes using a 240 V supply at 4.5 kW, with 80% reached in 64 minutes. Charging from a standard 120 V outlet is limited to 1.8 kW, so those faster times won’t apply.
Anker claims up to 10,000 battery cycles, although the supplied specifications do not state the remaining capacity at that point. The warranty runs for five years.
ESS News
will follow with a detailed review, including a closer look at usable capacity, charging, idle consumption, and how practical a 44 kg power station is to move around.

title: Batteries beat gas peakers on cost globally, but U.S. faces trade headwinds - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Four-hour storage is now cheaper than open-cycle gas in 43 modeled markets, though tariffs threaten near-term U.S. gains, said a report from Wood Mackenzie.
Ryan Kennedy
12 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
The levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) for four-hour battery storage has crossed a critical threshold, falling below open-cycle gas turbines across all 43 global markets modeled by Wood Mackenzie. However, while expanding manufacturing and volatile fuel prices drive gas peaking out of the market globally, North America faces a distinct trajectory marked by near-term trade barriers, policy shifts, and surging power demand from data centers.
Advancing technologies and manufacturing scale are redrawing global power market dynamics. Wood Mackenzie’s latest Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE) report shows that single-axis tracker solar is now the lowest-cost new-build power source in 43 of 48 modeled markets, with four-hour battery storage decisively beating open-cycle gas turbines on cost.
“This economic shift is decisive and widening,” said Ahmed Jameel Abdullah, principal analyst at Wood Mackenzie. “Gas turbine shortages and rising fuel volatility are driving up peaking costs, while expanding battery manufacturing continues to push storage costs down.”
Yet, North America stands out as a key exception in long-term cost trajectories, heavily influenced by domestic trade policies, supply chain protections, and load pressures.
Tariffs, data centers, and tax incentives
Unlike international markets benefiting from low-cost Chinese equipment exports, North American clean energy developers face immediate cost headwinds. Near-term solar costs across the U.S. and Canada remain elevated under a wave of tariffs, anti-dumping and countervailing duty (AD/CVD) actions, and Section 232 import restrictions.
Utility-scale solar developers maintain a buffer thanks to 168 GW of safe-harbored capacity, but module prices are still projected to climb ~5% annually through 2030. Distributed generation bears the brunt of the pressure, with residential and commercial solar module prices forecast to jump 6% in 2027 and an additional 14% in 2028.
For energy storage, Federal tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) continue to provide a critical competitive advantage, helping offset strict Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) sourcing restrictions and domestic supply bottlenecks. While a temporary cost increase is anticipated when the Investment Tax Credit (ITC) phases out in the late 2030s, hardware commoditization, alternative cell chemistries, and localized manufacturing expansion are expected to drive long-term storage LCOE down 10% by 2060.
Simultaneously, massive load growth from AI and data center development is forcing utilities to re-evaluate capacity planning. Thermal capital costs remain elevated due to a supply deficit cycle in gas generation equipment through the late 2030s, strengthening the long-term economic case for paired renewables and storage despite near-term headwinds.
Overseas markets pull ahea
Outside North America, global storage and solar costs are declining at a faster rate due to unhindered supply chain integration:
Middle East & Africa: Utility-scale single-axis solar leads globally at $37/MWh, on track to drop below $20/MWh in Saudi Arabia and the UAE by 2033. Four-hour battery storage sits at $120/MWh in 2026 and is forecast to fall 33% to $80/MWh by 2035, displacing open-cycle gas peaking across every gas market in the region.
Asia Pacific: China remains the global cost anchor with a grid-scale storage benchmark LCOE more than 55% below the rest of the APAC average ($134/MWh). Competitive Chinese exports are expected to drag the regional average down to $92/MWh by 2036, though tariff-heavy markets like Japan and Australia will maintain a premium.
Europe: High levelized carbon costs—projected to pass fuel costs by 2030—make Europe the most expensive region for fossil-fuel generation. Turnkey battery storage capex saw a minor 2% uptick in 2026 following a 10% cell price rebound, but costs are projected to fall 12% by 2031.
Latin America: Driven by top-tier solar irradiation, single-axis tracker solar leads all generation sources. Grid-scale battery storage LCOE is forecast to plunge 42% by 2060, supported by regional storage mandates and grid stability procurement.
Looking ahead
The convergence of falling storage costs and high gas turbine prices is shifting how grid operators plan baseline and peaking capacity. While North American developers must navigate trade restrictions and high load demand, the underlying economics continue to favor renewable-plus-storage builds over new thermal peaking plants.
“The structural shift we are tracking is no longer just about renewables becoming competitive,” Abdullah said. “It is about storage and solar together redefining what the economics of a power system look like. The combination of falling storage costs and world-class renewable resources is closing off the economic case for new gas peaking capacity globally.”

title: China turns toxic desalination waste into high-value chemical salt
content: A large-scale desalination facility in the Caofeidian industrial zone of Tangshan, Hebei province (China), has entered trial production. Designed through a collaboration between Tangshan Sanyou Group and academic experts, the plant operates on a circular model that reclaims valuable chemical raw materials from toxic waste brine at a fraction of standard energy costs.The facility reportedly cuts power demands by 60 percent and turns millions of tonnes of waste brine from desalination runoff into chemical salt.Ultimately, this innovation transforms hazardous desalination waste into a profitable manufacturing resource, offering a long-term cure for marine pollution in Bohai Bay.Closed-loop innovationDesalination facilities extract pure water from seawater using technologies like reverse osmosis, which separates the water molecules from the rest of the ocean water. Since a major portion of the liquid is removed, the remaining solution retains all the original dissolved salts, heavy minerals, and cleaning chemicals in a much smaller volume. This dense, hyper-saline discharge forms the toxic waste stream known as brine, carrying a concentration high enough to damage marine environments if dumped directly back into the ocean.The South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported that the plant treats waste brine using a three-to-one conversion ratio. Rather than pumping toxic discharge into fragile ecosystems, the plant operates on a strict circular model. For every three tonnes (3.3 U.S. tons) of raw waste brine processed, it yields two tonnes (2.2 U.S. tons) of fresh water and one tonne (1.1 U.S. tons) of hyper-concentrated brine with a salinity of 120 grams per liter.This refined solution travels through a 50-kilometer (31 miles) pipeline to a nearby chemical plant, where it serves as raw material to produce soda ash for glass, metallurgy, paper, textiles, and food manufacturing. Zhao Lin, head of R&D at Tangshan Sanyou Group, noted that the project is the “largest” and most energy-efficient of its kind worldwide.Speaking to Science and Technology Daily, Zhao explained that the plant uses 60 percent less electricity than standard desalination methods for generate 10,000 yuan (US$1,490) in economic value. Specialized membrane componentsAchieving this also required tackling challenges such as limescale.Normally, concentrating brine to extreme levels causes minerals like calcium, magnesium, and sulfate to precipitate violently. These minerals block pipes and crush fragile filtration equipment, like limescale in a hot kettle.Researchers also faced the complex economic and technical task of keeping the salt contained inside the brine throughout the process. To overcome this, researchers at Tangshan Sanyou Group designed a four-stage process using specialized membrane components that selectively filter out calcium and magnesium while preserving pure sodium chloride.The project involves financial and environmental benefits. Conventional techniques rely on extreme pressure to push water through highly saline membranes, driving up power costs and damaging machinery. Tangshan Sanyou avoids using force through a multi-stage approach, resulting in operational savings.Once the project reaches its third phase, the plant will process nearly 100 million tonnes (110 million U.S. tons) of concentrated seawater annually. That single facility could permanently relieve Bohai Bay of one of its heaviest industrial burdens.Global initiatives currently operate mostly at pilot or research levels, making the Tangshan facility uniquely advanced due to its massive scale, direct connection to heavy soda ash manufacturing, and power cuts. Saudi Arabia, as the world’s leading producer of desalinated water, invests through NEOM and the Saline Water Conversion Corporation (SWCC) in Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) and brine-mining infrastructure. The projects focus on extracting high-purity sodium chloride, magnesium, and lithium from concentrated discharge to supply domestic chemical sectors.

title: Worm-like robot shifts water inside its body to cross land and sea
content: Researchers at New York University have developed a worm-like robot designed to navigate rugged coastal terrain. Called WorMa, the robot can move across rocks and slopes before entering and exiting water.Its design is inspired by the way worms adapt their movement to changing environments. The researchers developed the robot to tackle terrain that can be difficult for conventional wheeled or legged machines.Water-powered weight shiftResearchers at NYU’s Tandon School of Engineering developed WorMa, an amphibious, worm-like robot that changes how it moves across different terrain by shifting its weight. Instead of switching between entirely different gaits or mechanically reconfiguring its body, the robot uses water as a movable ballast. A pump transfers water between tanks in its head and tail, allowing WorMa to redistribute its mass and adjust how it interacts with the ground or water.WorMa is designed to handle transitions between surfaces that can challenge conventional robots. The five-link, four-joint robot is about 20 inches long (50 centimeters) long and weighs slightly more than 2.2 pounds (1 kilogram). Its body contains latex water balloons at the head and tail, while a pump located in the middle section moves about 10.6 ounces (about 300 grams) of water between them.The technology relies on changing the robot’s center of mass rather than adding specialized mechanical components for each environment. Moving the water toward the head increases the force applied through the front contact points. This gives the robot greater traction when climbing sloped surfaces. During testing, the head-heavy configuration allowed WorMa to climb an incline as steep as 19.5 degrees, while other weight configurations caused it to slide backward. The configuration also reduced the robot’s cost of transport by at least 33 percent compared with the alternatives tested.The same weight-shifting mechanism produces a different effect in water. Moving the water toward the tail improves the robot’s swimming performance by changing its mass distribution. In tests, the tail-heavy configuration allowed WorMa to swim up to 26 percent faster and operate 52 percent more efficiently than when its weight was concentrated toward the head.WorMa tackles terrainThe robot uses a more complex sequence to overcome steps. It first approaches with its water concentrated in the head to maintain traction. The pump then moves the water toward the tail, causing the front section to rise and allowing the tail to push the robot closer to the obstacle. Once the head establishes contact with the step’s edge, water is transferred back toward the head, helping the robot anchor itself and continue forward. Using this sequence, WorMa cleared steps about 6 inches (up to 15 centimeters) high.According to the team, the same principle helps the robot leave water. With its mass concentrated toward the head, WorMa can generate enough force at its front section to pull itself onto a slope. Other tested configurations could not produce sufficient traction for the transition.The researchers demonstrated the robot crossing a course containing flat ground, a step, a slope, and open water. WorMa adjusted its mass distribution for each section while maintaining its basic undulatory movement pattern.“What it gives you is a robot that doesn’t need to be redesigned every time the terrain changes. That could matter for environmental monitoring or infrastructure inspection, where a robot may need to cross dry ground, obstacles, and water during the same mission,” said Nana Obayashi, an assistant professor at Tandon, in a statement. The approach could simplify amphibious robots by replacing multiple specialized mechanisms with a single adaptable mass-shifting system. The researchers are also working on faster pumps and sensor-based controls that could let WorMa detect terrain changes and automatically redistribute its weight. This could eventually enable the robot to adapt more dynamically while operating in environments such as coastlines, wetlands, and flooded areas.

title: 3x faster clean energy generation recorded from energy-importing countries
content: A new report has revealed that energy-importing countries are scaling clean energy generation three times faster than exporters. The disruption to energy supply through the Strait of Hormuz is reinforcing governments’ determination to reduce dependence on imported oil and gas, according to the tenth edition of DNV’s Energy Transition Outlook.At the same time, exporting countries outside the Middle East are increasing production to compensate for disrupted supplies, whilst their own decarbonization journeys are increasingly slower compared to the rest of the world.Share of non-fossil energyAs a result, the share of non-fossil energy in the primary energy mix of importing regions increased by 2.2 percentage points over the past five years, compared with just 0.7 percentage points in exporting regions. This means China, India and Europe have collectively shifted towards non-fossil energy more than three times as fast as the Middle East, North America and Russia, according to the report.“Energy security is redrawing the map of the energy transition,” said Ditlev Engel, CEO – Energy Systems at DNV. “Importing regions are accelerating electrification, renewables and storage to reduce their exposure to the most insecure fossil-fuel markets. Exporters, meanwhile, are responding to today’s shortages by increasing investments and production. The result is a widening divide in the speed and direction of the transition.”The disruption to the Strait of Hormuz has strengthened incentives for importing countries to diversify supply and reduce their exposure to oil and gas, increasing the long-term risks facing fossil-a exporters. DNV’s new forecast sees the Middle East supplying around 40% of global oil production in 2050, compared with 50% in last year’s outlook, according to a press release.An additional DNV sensitivity analysis examines the impact of the Middle East conflict continuing until 2030, with oil and gas prices remaining moderately elevated during that period. Under this scenario, global oil and gas demand would be 4–6% lower while the conflict persists. Demand would remain 2–5% below DNV’s main forecast for the remainder of the forecast period, indicating permanent demand destruction as consumers and governments accelerate the shift to alternative energy sources, as per the release.“While the geopolitical landscape is becoming more complex, there should be no doubt that the energy transition is happening, and that it is already large in scale. However, we must continue to embrace and accelerate it, as everyone is starting to recognize that energy is now part of our critical infrastructure and must be prioritized accordingly,” added Engel.The report also revealed that the gap is widening between competitive mature technologies and emerging technologies reliant on increasingly constrained policy support. Falling costs are accelerating the deployment of solar power, onshore wind and batteries, whilst more expensive emerging technologies are losing ground. Solar PV and onshore wind are increasingly displacing fossil fuels from power generation, and installed battery capacity has increased 14-fold over the past five years.Decarbonizing the hard-to-electrify sectorsThe report also highlighted that the technologies essential to decarbonizing the hard-to-electrify sectors are not being prioritized due to their high cost and concerns about industrial competitiveness. Compared to last year’s outlook, the amount of hydrogen and carbon capture and storage in DNV’s long-term forecast are down 29% and 15% respectively. While both technologies are still expected to grow rapidly from a low base, stronger policy support will be needed to bridge the cost gap and accelerate deployment.Nuclear power is the notable exception among higher-cost technologies. DNV forecasts that nuclear will maintain its current share of global power generation as electrification accelerates. Installed nuclear capacity is expected to grow by 30% over the next decade and by 170% by 2060, despite high costs and supply-chain risks.“Driven by solar, wind and increasingly battery storage, electricity is emerging as the clear winner of the energy transition,” said Sverre Alvik, Director of Energy Transition Research at DNV. “The pace of electrification over the next two decades will be more than twice that of the past two decades. Although importing countries are leading the shift, fossil-fuel exporters are also embracing electrification because it delivers greater efficiency and lower costs.”

title: BYD’s humanoid robot has 31 degrees of freedom and a dexterous hand
content: Chinese automaker BYD has unveiled the design of its first self-developed humanoid robot, marking a broader push into embodied AI and robotics that could eventually see the company deploy autonomous machines across its factories and dealerships.The design appeared in a patent published by China’s National Intellectual Property Administration, describing a robot designed to walk, maintain balance and interact with its surroundings.The patent points to potential applications in service, education and industrial environments. Although the design resembles BYD’s previously teased humanoid robot, known as Xiao Di, the company has not confirmed whether the patent depicts the final production model.Designed for real-world interactionThe newly revealed design features a black-and-white body, a rounded head without a display and articulated joints across its torso, arms and legs. Its human-like proportions suggest a platform intended to operate in environments designed for people, rather than a robot restricted to a dedicated industrial workspace.Previously disclosed specifications for the Xiao Di concept put its height at approximately 5 feet 3 inches and its weight at around 129 pounds (58 kg). The robot is reported to have 31 degrees of freedom, allowing movement across multiple joints, and a dexterous hand with repeatable positioning accuracy of approximately 0.04 inches.These features could support tasks such as picking up objects, making gestures and pointing out information to people. However, the published design does not establish how reliably the robot can perform these tasks in real-world conditions, or whether the specifications will carry over to a production model.As automakers and technology companies invest in embodied AI, which combines AI with physical systems that can sense and interact with the real world, humanoid robots face a more complex challenge than software-based AI. They must coordinate perception, decision-making and physical movement while maintaining balance and adapting to changing environments. BYD is looking to apply its manufacturing expertise in developing such robots.Developing its robotics capabilities for yearsBYD’s humanoid robot project is part of a longer-term research effort that began in 2022 with the formation of a dedicated team tasked with developing the hardware and software needed to bring embodied AI into practical use. It has also invested in other companies in the sector. BYD invested in Agibot in August 2023 and acquired a stake in Percibot in April 2025, expanding its connections to China’s developing robotics industry.The company has also explored industrial applications through its manufacturing operations. Its Changsha factory has hosted Ubtech’s Walker S1 humanoid robot for material-handling and identification tasks, providing an example of how humanoid systems could be tested in real production environments.BYD executives have previously indicated that the company could deploy humanoid robots across its dealership network, with potential tasks including greeting customers, explaining vehicle features and demonstrating infotainment systems. Such applications would give BYD a way to test whether humanoid robots can perform routine customer-facing work without requiring major changes to existing facilities.For now, BYD has yet to announce a production timeline or confirm whether the newly published design represents the final version of its Xiao Di humanoid robot, leaving open questions about its commercial launch and which capabilities will make it into a production model.

title: US Coast Guard to add MQ-9B drones with 30-hour flight time to fleet
content: The U.S. Coast Guard has ordered four MQ-9B long-range unmanned aircraft from General Atomics in a $247.8 million deal. Built by General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, the MQ-9B has a 79-foot wingspan and can operate in civilian airspace.Also called the SeaGuardian, the MQ-9B is a remotely piloted aircraft equipped with specialized sensors for wide-area maritime radar, an automatic identification system, electronic support measures, and an anti-submarine warfare mission kit.The aircraft can remain airborne for more than 30 hours and communicate beyond the horizon via satellite. According to General Atomics, the SkyGuardian’s capabilities are highly robust. It can conduct search and rescue, law enforcement, anti-surface warfare, anti-submarine warfare, and long-range intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions.Drawn by this impressive array of functionalities, the U.S. Coast Guard placed an order through a U.S. Customs and Border Protection contract, according to a U.S. Coast Guard press release.The U.S. Coast Guard goes high-techThe U.S. Coast Guard oversees more than 95,000 miles of shoreline, 25,000 miles of navigable rivers, and 4.5 million square miles of the U.S. exclusive economic zone, so it has a vast area to monitor. The Coast Guard used an earlier version of the MQ-9A aircraft in maritime counter-drug operations. These operations enabled authorities to seize about 60,700 pounds of illegal drugs in 2026. The seized narcotics were valued at approximately $306 million, and the operations contributed to the apprehension of around 20 smugglers.The Coast Guard cited these results as proof that these long-range unmanned aircraft deliver. It’s no wonder they ordered the latest edition. The newly acquired MQ-9B systems are intended to expand the service’s ability to collect and share intelligence, identify potential threats, and support reconnaissance missions over offshore waters.The MQ-9B aircraft will improve the Coast Guard’s ability to monitor offshore waters, protect borders and critical infrastructure, support search and rescue, combat drug trafficking, and counter illegal and unregulated fishing. “The MQ-9B long-range unmanned aircraft systems will expand our reach and strengthen our ability to protect the nation,” said Anthony Antognoli, assistant commandant and program executive officer for Robotics and Autonomous Systems.“This investment will give Coast Guard crews a longer-range view of our maritime domain, helping them detect threats earlier, make better-informed decisions and act faster across our missions.”Nearly $25 billionThe Coast Guard currently operates more than 220 cutters, 185 fixed- and rotary-wing aircraft, and 1,300 boats, according to the press release. According to the U.S. Coast Guard, the new aircraft acquisition was funded by a “historic investment” of nearly $25 billion. That funding allocated about $16.3 billion for new assets and capabilities to modernize acquisitions, integrate new technologies, restore operational readiness, and improve infrastructure.Its responsibilities include maritime border security, drug interdiction, the protection of ports and waterways, and the safeguarding of the nation’s 4.5 million square miles of exclusive economic zone. The four MQ-9B aircraft will add long-range unmanned surveillance capabilities to those operations as the service continues its modernization efforts.The Coast Guard’s announcement did not specify a delivery schedule or state when the new aircraft are expected to enter operational service.

title: Experimental Heart Drug Helps Patients Exercise More and Feel Better
content:
An experimental drug designed to reduce excessive heart muscle contraction helped patients with a difficult-to-treat form of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy exercise more effectively. Credit: Stock
In a new trial, an experimental drug helped patients with an inherited heart muscle condition feel better and exercise more.
Two new studies found that aficamten improved exercise capacity and reported health in people with nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (nHCM). This inherited condition thickens and stiffens the heart muscle, often causing shortness of breath and limiting physical activity.
Aficamten reduces the activity of cardiac myosin, a protein that helps the heart muscle contract. The studies, published in
The New England Journal of Medicine
Circulation
, tested whether easing those contractions could benefit patients with nHCM, who account for about 30 percent of people with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Patients Felt Better and Exercised More
In the trial reported in
The New England Journal of Medicine
, 517 participants received aficamten or a placebo. After 36 weeks, the aficamten group showed greater improvements in both reported health status and peak oxygen consumption, a measure of how much oxygen the body can use during intense exercise.
Patients with nHCM have lacked a treatment targeted to the condition, said Lubna Choudhury, MD, a professor of Medicine in the Division of Cardiology and a co-author of both studies. “With these new studies, I can now recommend to patients a specific designer drug therapy which can work for them, make them feel better, and also improve their overall heart failure status.”
The measured gain in exercise capacity helped show that the benefit extended beyond how patients described their symptoms. “This was a game changer, because that really shows we can impact these patients, not only in the way they feel, but objectively in the cardiac function that we’re measuring with the peak VO
,” Choudhury said.
Heart Scans Offer A Possible Explanation
The companion
Circulation
study analyzed heart ultrasound scans taken throughout the trial. Compared with placebo, aficamten reduced signs of excessive contraction and improved several measures of diastolic function, the heart’s ability to relax and fill with blood between beats.
Researchers also found improved tissue Doppler measurements of how the heart muscle relaxes, changes in blood volume within the left ventricle, and lower markers of cardiac stress. These findings raise the possibility that aficamten affects the underlying disease process as well as relieves symptoms, though longer follow-up is needed to determine whether the changes last.
“We saw indications from the
Circulation
paper that diastolic dysfunction parameters improve. That may explain why the patients feel better,” Choudhury said.
Longer Follow-Up Will Test The Benefits
The trial built on
earlier evidence
that aficamten helps people with obstructive HCM. Researchers wanted to learn whether those benefits would extend to patients without an outflow tract obstruction, who have historically had no targeted treatment options.
The benefits also came with a reason for careful monitoring. In the nHCM trial, a reversible decline in a measure of the heart’s pumping ability occurred more often with aficamten than with the placebo.
An ongoing extension study is following people with both forms of HCM to assess aficamten’s effects over a longer period. “We want to get more long-term data on how these things look after several years in these patients,” Choudhury said.

title: A Powerful Diet and Exercise Combination Sends Type 2 Diabetes Into Remission
content:
Researchers have identified a promising approach to early-onset type 2 diabetes that may protect muscle while improving metabolic health. Its long-term implications could reshape treatment strategies. Credit: Shutterstock
A low-calorie diet and exercise program helped over half its participants reach remission from early-onset type 2 diabetes at 24 weeks while preserving muscle.
A falling number on the bathroom scale can hide a difficult trade-off for someone trying to put type 2 diabetes into remission, since the body may be losing muscle along with fat. For people diagnosed before age 45, protecting that muscle adds another challenge to treating a form of diabetes that tends to worsen quickly, cause complications earlier, and shorten life expectancy compared with diabetes that develops later.
In the RESET for Remission trial, researchers at three centers in England and Canada paired a diet of 800 to 900 calories a day with structured exercise to address both problems. After 24 weeks, 27 of the 50 participants following the program, or 54%, had achieved remission, bringing their blood sugar below the diabetes diagnostic threshold without glucose-lowering medication. Among the 46 participants receiving usual care, two, or 4%, achieved remission.
The team included Professor Kaberi Dasgupta, director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University in Montreal, Quebec, Canada, and Professor Thomas Yates of the University of Leicester in the United Kingdom. They worked with colleagues at the trial’s three participating centers, which were affiliated with McGill, Leicester, and the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada.
The 96 participants were randomly assigned to the combined program or usual care between September 24, 2021, and June 6, 2025. All were between 18 and 45 years old, had early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity, and were not taking insulin. Forty participants were from the United Kingdom and 56 were from Canada. Their average age was 38, and their average body mass index was 35.2 kilograms per square meter.
Twenty-four female and 26 male participants entered the intervention group, while 21 female and 25 male participants received usual care. Participants knew which treatment they were receiving, making this an open-label trial, but the people assessing the study endpoints were kept unaware of those assignments.
The authors said, “Our remission rates are at the upper end of those previously reported in the literature for trials of similar duration, reinforcing the potential of structured lifestyle interventions to support clinically meaningful remission, while demonstrating for the first time that such effects can be achieved in a multi-ethnic population with early onset type 2 diabetes through a combined low energy diet and structured exercise intervention.”
Cutting calories while keeping muscles working
For the first two weeks, participants in the intervention group replaced all meals with
Optifast
products. Their daily intake of 800 to 900 calories was divided into 30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, and 20% fat. Under the trial protocol, participants stopped glucose- and blood pressure-lowering medications when the diet began, in the absence of albuminuria, or albumin protein in the urine.
Alongside those restricted menus, participants completed two supervised exercise sessions and one independent session each week during the first 12 weeks. The supervised program combined aerobic and resistance exercise, which the researchers expected could complement the diet by improving fitness and heart function, preserving muscle, and reducing insulin resistance. Insulin resistance occurs when the body responds poorly to the hormone that helps regulate blood sugar.
Eighty-six participants, or 90% of those enrolled, attended the final assessments. The researchers included everyone who had been randomized in their primary analyses of effectiveness and harms, counting anyone with missing remission data as not having achieved remission. After statistical adjustment, they reported that participants in the combined program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving usual care. They also assessed cardiorespiratory fitness, body composition, and the structure of the heart.
The authors said, “Our findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low energy diet in early-onset type 2 diabetes, supporting its potential to deliver substantial and holistic health and well-being benefits alongside diabetes remission.”
More fat lost, muscle preserved
Among the 47 intervention participants included in the reported weight figures, average weight fell from 100.7 kilograms at the start to 92.3 kilograms at week 24. That was a loss of 8.4 kilograms, or about 18.5 pounds. The corresponding figures for 43 control participants showed a decline from 103.2 to 102.0 kilograms, a loss of 1.2 kilograms, or about 2.6 pounds.
After statistical adjustment, participants in the combined program lost an average of 7.5 kilograms, about 16.5 pounds, more than those receiving usual care. That difference included an additional 6.6 kilograms, about 14.6 pounds, of fat mass lost. The researchers also reported preservation of fat-free mass and muscle, addressing the concern that rapid weight loss could take away tissue participants would benefit from keeping.
Forty-three of the 50 intervention participants experienced at least one adverse event, compared with six of the 46 people receiving usual care. These were mainly early effects of the low-energy diet, including constipation, headache, dizziness, and fatigue, which resolved. No severe adverse events occurred.
Weight regain may favor fat over muscle
People who lose weight through dietary programs, including low-energy diets intended to bring about diabetes remission, commonly regain some or all of it, the authors noted. Lowering food intake alone can reduce both fat and fat-free mass, which includes muscle. Some evidence suggests that when weight returns, the body may restore fat more readily than fat-free mass, leaving people with a net loss of fat-free tissue and a greater risk of sarcopenia, a condition involving declining muscle mass and function, over time.
The RESET team said, “Our RESET for Remission study targeted muscle during the intensive weight loss phase through resistance training, and our findings indicate fat-free mass and muscle preservation is achievable with rapid weight loss. Preserving muscle during remission-oriented weight loss may have important implications for long-term metabolic health, physical function, and disease trajectory. This requires examination in a longer-term study.”
The team’s findings were published in
The Lancet Regional Health Americas
. The researchers focused on early-onset type 2 diabetes as a distinct and growing clinical population whose rapid disease progression calls for an intervention capable of interrupting it.
The authors concluded, “By focusing specifically on early-onset type 2 diabetes, our trial addresses a growing clinical population, characterized by elevated cardiovascular disease risk, greater cumulative complication burden, and poor long-term outcomes…In summary, RESET for Remission demonstrated that in early-onset type 2 diabetes, combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low-calorie diet produces high remission rates, induces fat loss while preserving muscle mass, improves muscle quality and function, enhances cardiovascular health, and leads to meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes. As the prevalence of early-onset type 2 diabetes rises globally, our findings highlight an opportunity to re-evaluate treatment paradigms and support scalable implementation of integrated dietary and exercise interventions for remission. Our approach may be particularly valuable in those seeking or with potential for pregnancy. It warrants further evaluation in longer-term studies in real-world settings.”
Following people beyond 24 weeks will be needed to establish how long remission lasts and whether preserving muscle changes their health over the years that follow. For someone watching the number on the bathroom scale fall, the longer-term question is what keeping that muscle could mean when the intensive diet ends and, as happens for many people, some of the weight returns.

title: Beyond Ozempic? New Weight Loss Drug Shows Stunning Results in Major Clinical Trial
content:
A drug targeting three hormone pathways also improved several markers of cardiovascular and metabolic health (Artist’s concept). Credit: Stock
Retatrutide could help tackle obesity and type 2 diabetes together, with an 80-week trial showing substantial weight loss and better blood sugar control alongside more nausea and diarrhea.
A weekly injection beneath the skin helped adults with excess weight and type 2 diabetes lose nearly a fifth of their starting weight, on average, at the highest dose tested. That is a substantial shift on the scale for a population that has generally lost less weight with obesity medications than people without diabetes.
Researchers tested the investigational drug retatrutide over 80 weeks in TRIUMPH-2, a completed phase 3 trial involving 1,152 adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes. Participants received weekly injections of the drug or a placebo, alongside dietary counseling and guidance on physical activity. Eli Lilly, which manufactures retatrutide, sponsored the study, and the findings were published in
The Lancet
Retatrutide activates three types of hormone receptors, the molecular receiving points through which cells respond to signals. It targets receptors for glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP), glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), and glucagon, making it a “triple agonist.” Researchers are investigating whether this approach can improve both weight and blood sugar control in people who need help managing the two together.
Weight loss rises with retatrutide dose
Participants entered the trial having lived with obesity for a median of 21 years and diabetes for a median of 5.6 years. At randomization, 92% were taking at least one oral glucose-lowering medication, including biguanides, SGLT-2 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, and other oral treatments.
“There is an unmet need for more efficacious weight reduction in individuals with obesity and type 2 diabetes…Findings from TRIUMPH-2 suggest that retatrutide may advance the treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes, a population where weight reduction has been challenging to achieve,” the authors write.
Blood tests tracked those changes alongside HbA1c, a measure that reflects average blood sugar over the preceding few months. From a mean starting HbA1c of 7.71%, the average reductions at week 80 were 1.38 percentage points with retatrutide 4 mg, 1.50 percentage points with 9 mg, and 1.45 percentage points with 12 mg. The placebo group’s average reduction was 0.45 percentage points.
Among participants receiving 12 mg, 72% reached an HbA1c of 6.5% or lower, compared with 29% receiving placebo. Retatrutide also significantly improved cardiometabolic risk factors, including blood pressure and lipid profiles, and reduced high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, or hsCRP, a marker of inflammation.
Medical and research centers and hospitals at 92 sites across eight countries participated in the trial: Argentina, Australia, Brazil, India, Mexico, Romania, Spain, and the United States. Adults were eligible if they were at least 18 years old, had a body mass index (BMI) of at least 27 kg/m², and had type 2 diabetes with an HbA1c between 6.5% and 10.5%.
Investigators screened 2,047 people before randomly assigning 1,152 participants to the four treatment groups. Each participant had an equal chance of receiving placebo or one of the three retatrutide doses, all administered by subcutaneous injection, meaning beneath the skin. The final assignments were 292 participants to 4 mg, 284 to 9 mg, 287 to 12 mg, and 289 to placebo.
Participants had a mean age of 55.1 years and a mean BMI of 38.2 kg/m². The reported sex breakdown was 554 female participants, or 48%, and 592 male participants, or 52%. The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial used percentage change in body weight at week 80 as its primary endpoint, with change in HbA1c at the same time point as a key secondary endpoint. Of those randomized, 1,046 participants, or 91%, completed the study, including 965 participants, or 84%, who completed it while still receiving their assigned study treatment.
Study co-author Dr. Juan Pablo Frías, medical director and principal investigator at the Los Angeles Institute for Metabolic Research in Los Angeles, California, was scheduled to present the study design and efficacy results at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, September 28 to October 2.
More nausea and diarrhea with retatrutide
Diarrhea and nausea were among the gastrointestinal adverse events reported most frequently, and both occurred more often with retatrutide. Across the three drug groups, diarrhea affected 27% to 34% of participants, or 80 to 96 people per group, compared with 13%, or 38 people, receiving placebo. Nausea affected 14% to 28%, or 40 to 80 people per retatrutide group, compared with 8%, or 23 people, receiving placebo.
Participants also experienced episodes of hypotension, meaning abnormally low blood pressure, orthostatic hypotension, a drop in blood pressure upon standing, or decreased blood pressure. These events occurred in 1% of participants receiving 4 mg, 5% receiving 9 mg, and 6% receiving 12 mg, compared with less than 1% receiving placebo.
Abnormal skin sensations, such as burning or discomfort, were reported as dysesthesia in 4%, 6%, and 7% of participants receiving retatrutide 4 mg, 9 mg, and 12 mg, respectively. The corresponding figure with placebo was 1%. None of these events were classified as severe or serious.
Adverse events or death led to permanent treatment discontinuation in 12% of participants receiving 9 mg, or 33 people, and 8% receiving 12 mg, or 22 people. The figures were lower in the 4 mg group, at 4%, or 11 people, and in the placebo group, at 5%, or 14 people.
Seven participants died during the study: two in the 4 mg group, three in the 9 mg group, one in the 12 mg group, and one in the placebo group. The investigator deemed the deaths unrelated to the study intervention.
“Retatrutide demonstrated substantial reduction in body weight alongside improvements in blood sugar control and cardiometabolic risk factors, with a safety profile generally similar to other molecules with GLP-1 receptor agonist activity,” the authors conclude. “These findings support obesity treatment as a strategy for people with obesity and type 2 diabetes.”
Retatrutide’s broader health benefits remain uncertain
Researchers are also investigating retatrutide for other obesity-related complications, including cardiovascular disease, metabolic liver disease, knee osteoarthritis, chronic low back pain, and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Those investigations extend beyond the weight and blood sugar outcomes assessed here.
The weekly injection beneath the skin may eventually be judged by more than the weight it takes off the scale. As the authors write, “Further studies are required to determine whether these benefits translate to improvements in other obesity-related complications.”

title: Scientists Discover a Strange New Quantum State Where Two Materials Meet
content:
Artistic illustration of electrons interacting at the interface between a one-atom-thick material and a metal, forming an unusual heavy-fermion quantum state through interactions between localized and mobile electrons. Credit: Takuto Nakamura
Researchers have directly observed an unusual quantum state emerging at the boundary between an atomically thin material and a metal.
Scientists have directly observed an unusual quantum state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. The discovery, made by a research team led by the
University of Osaka
, demonstrates how interactions between electrons in different materials can produce a state known as a heavy fermion, potentially offering new ways to engineer quantum materials.
Heavy-fermion states occur when strong interactions cause electrons to behave as if they have unusually large effective masses. These states are closely associated with exotic quantum phenomena, including unconventional superconductivity, in which electrical current can flow without resistance through mechanisms that differ from those in conventional superconductors.
Two Distinct Quantum States at an Atomic Interface
To investigate how these states emerge, the researchers created a high-quality, one-atom-thick layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu₂) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used intense synchrotron light to examine the electronic structure of the combined materials and identify interactions occurring at their boundary.
The measurements revealed two separate heavy-fermion states. One was concentrated primarily within the two-dimensional YbCu₂ layer, while the other extended into the three-dimensional copper substrate. The second state formed through hybridization, a process in which localized ytterbium 4f electrons interact with mobile conduction electrons in the underlying metal. This provided the first direct experimental evidence of a heavy-fermion state arising from electronic interactions across such an interface.
Engineering Materials With New Quantum Properties
The results suggest that researchers could deliberately create and control heavy-electron states by combining carefully selected atomic layers with suitable substrates. Adjusting the atomic arrangement at the interface, the electronic orbitals involved, and moiré patterns formed by overlapping crystal lattices could make it possible to produce quantum behavior unavailable in conventional materials.
“This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible,” says senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. “Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity.”

title: Scientists Decode the Unusual Weather of a Planet 20 Light-Years From Earth
content:
An artistic depiction of SIMP 0136. Credit: Chuck Carter, NRAO/AUI/NSF
JWST observations reveal that the changing atmosphere of brown dwarf SIMP 0136 may be governed by just a few underlying processes.
A world 20 light-years from Earth appears to have a much more orderly atmosphere than its constantly changing clouds suggest.
Using observations from NASA’s
James Webb Space Telescope (JWST)
, scientists at
Trinity College Dublin
found that most of the atmospheric variability on the brown dwarf SIMP 0136 can be traced to just two dominant processes: changes in temperature and changes in the vertical structure of its clouds. Those processes appear to combine into three recurring weather states that rotate in and out of view.
The result offers a new way to separate the underlying physics of distant atmospheres from the complicated brightness changes astronomers actually observe. The study was published in
Astronomy & Astrophysics
Three Weather States Dominate the Atmosphere
SIMP 0136 is larger and hotter than a gas giant planet but does not have enough mass to sustain the hydrogen fusion that powers a star. Its atmosphere contains enormous, rapidly changing cloud systems, making it more comparable to an extreme version of Jupiter than to Earth.
As SIMP 0136 rotates, different regions of its atmosphere face Earth. JWST can detect extremely small changes in the object’s brightness across different wavelengths, allowing astronomers to infer how temperature and clouds vary across the visible hemisphere.
The new study indicates that much of this changing signal can be explained by three recurring atmospheric states. Some regions are hotter with thinner clouds, while others are cooler and contain thicker clouds that extend farther vertically through the atmosphere. Rather than reorganizing randomly, these broad atmospheric patterns persisted across more than a dozen rotations.
“We also discovered that these drivers of the weather patterns on SIMP-0136 persist over time, even as the detailed appearance of the atmosphere evolves over more than a dozen rotations,” said first author Merle Schrader, a PhD candidate in Trinity’s School of Physics.
Pulling Weather Patterns Directly From the Data
To identify the dominant atmospheric changes, the researchers used a statistical method called Principal Component Analysis (PCA). The technique reduces a complicated data set to a smaller number of patterns that account for most of its variation.
PCA allowed the researchers to identify which changes in SIMP 0136’s light tended to occur together. The two strongest components were consistent with variations in atmospheric temperature and cloud structure, while weaker fluctuations could be separated from those dominant signals and from random noise.
The approach differs from methods that begin with detailed assumptions about an atmosphere and then test whether a model reproduces the observations. Instead, PCA can first identify the major sources of variability present in the data, giving researchers a simpler starting point before they turn to more computationally intensive atmospheric models.
“In relative terms, SIMP 0136 is one of the easier brown dwarfs for us to capture high-quality data from. These data have been studied before by established methods, allowing us to compare some of the results from this new technique to what we already know about this object. The technique has also helped us develop a better understanding of what drives the weather on this faraway world and how these weather patterns interact and co-exist, but perhaps even more importantly, it shows how this approach can be further refined and applied to other, less well-known brown dwarfs in different parts of space.”
A Test Case for Distant Atmospheres
Brown dwarfs offer a clearer view of atmospheric processes such as cloud formation, circulation, and heat transport than most exoplanets, which are harder to observe directly. Studying SIMP 0136 could therefore help astronomers interpret the atmospheres of giant worlds beyond the Solar System.
“Our findings will transform how astronomers analyze future JWST observations. Since our approach rapidly identifies the dominant components of the atmosphere, it offers an efficient first step before we begin computationally intensive modeling,” said Prof. Johanna Vos, associate professor in Trinity School of Physics.
“Applying this technique to a wide range of brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets will help us better understand the diverse weather systems that shape worlds far beyond our Solar System.”
Twenty Years of Light in a Single Pixel
SIMP 0136 also provided an unusual coincidence for Schrader. The brown dwarf lies about 20 light-years away, meaning the light recorded by JWST in 2023 had been traveling through space for roughly two decades. It was emitted in the same year Schrader was born.
“Light travels at around 300,000 km/s but, even at that speed, it took two decades to reach us, peering through the JWST lenses,” she said.
That speed is about 186,000 miles per second. Light traveling from Earth reaches the Moon in a little more than a second.
“When you consider light takes just over a second to reach the Moon after leaving Earth, that gives a sense of how far away SIMP 0136 is, and how incredible astrophysical progress has been. I think it’s amazing that we have been able to discern the intimate weather patterns of a distant world and map their interactions from our cozy little corner of the universe, when all we observe directly of these objects is a single pixel spread across the light spectrum.”
Extending the method to more brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets could help astronomers determine which atmospheric processes dominate on worlds with different temperatures, cloud compositions, and circulation patterns. Better measurements of those atmospheres can also improve understanding of their chemistry, an essential part of assessing the physical conditions present on distant planets.

title: Scientists Create a Nuclear Clock So Precise It Barely Loses a Second in 30 Million Years
content:
Scientists have created a self-stabilizing nuclear clock with a precision equivalent to one second in 30 million years, potentially paving the way for the most accurate clocks ever built. (Artist’s concept.) Credit: SciTechDaily.com
A self-stabilizing nuclear clock has achieved precision equivalent to roughly one second in 30 million years, though it still trails the best optical atomic clocks.
For a clock that keeps time with laser light, even a slight shift in the laser’s frequency changes its rhythm. Researchers in Vienna have now built the world’s first nuclear clock that automatically corrects those shifts, using thorium nuclei as its reference. It remained stable for more than 24 hours without intervention, achieving the self-regulation already customary in atomic clocks.
Measurements over the course of a day put the prototype’s precision at approximately 10⁻¹⁵, corresponding to an error of roughly one second in 30 million years. “This is not yet at the level of the world’s best optical atomic clocks, but for a first prototype it is a fantastic result,” says Professor Thorsten Schumm of the Institute of Atomic and Subatomic Physics at TU Wien.
The thorium crystal and the laser beam. Credit: TU Wien
Thorium nuclei respond to laser light
The clock is built around a crystal containing thorium atoms, produced at TU Wien and illuminated with a laser. “The oscillation of this laser light can be used for timekeeping, but the laser frequency can shift slightly from time to time, for example due to temperature fluctuations,” Schumm explains. “For high-precision measurements, you therefore need a mechanism to keep the laser frequency exactly stable, so that the clock continues to tick with precisely the same rhythm.”
Conventional atomic clocks use the energy states of electrons in atoms to establish that reference. Thorium offers a different possibility that scientists had suspected for decades: two of its nuclear energy states lie exceptionally close together. The gap is small enough for laser light to move the nucleus from one state to the other. Other atomic nuclei have much larger energy gaps, preventing laser light from driving such transitions.
Luca Toscani de Col (top right) working on the nuclear clock in the Vienna lab. Credit: Matthias Heisler, TU Wien
A nuclear clock that tunes itself
After decades of work toward nuclear clocks by researchers around the world, Schumm’s team and a team led by Professor Ekkehard Peik at PTB Braunschweig demonstrated laser excitation of thorium nuclei for the first time in April 2024. That fall, the team coupled the thorium excitation apparatus to a conventional optical atomic clock and used the nuclei as a timekeeper, demonstrating that they could support a high-precision clock.
That earlier setup had not yet achieved the self-stabilization needed to pursue precision records. “What you really want is a self-stabilizing nuclear clock,” Schumm explains. “The basic idea is simple: you have a laser, and you have thorium. The laser changes the energy state of the thorium nuclei, and the thorium nuclei are used to stabilize the frequency of the laser.”
The thorium nuclei absorb laser light at the correct frequency, and even a slight departure from that frequency produces a measurable drop in absorption. The new clock uses that drop to readjust the laser automatically, allowing it to stabilize itself without necessarily relying on a conventional atomic clock.
The TU Wien team: Thomas Riebner, Luca Toscani de Col, Thorsten Schumm, Fabian Schaden, Felix Schneider, Ira Morawetz (left to right). Credit: Matthias Heisler, TU Wien
Smaller nuclei, less outside interference
“The great advantage of the new nuclear clock in Vienna is that, if you use atomic nuclei rather than atoms, much higher precision is possible in principle,” says Schumm. Atomic nuclei are more than 10,000 times smaller than atoms and react much more weakly to external disturbances, making them more dependable timing references. That reduced sensitivity could eventually support measurements of a range of physical quantities with previously unattainable precision.
The team now aims to improve the prototype’s precision substantially with stronger lasers, better thorium crystals, and other measures.
Reference: “A thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with feedback loop” by L. Toscani De Col, T. Riebner, I. Morawetz, F. Schneider, N. Sempelmann, J. Schlachet-Lépinay, F. Schaden, M. Bartokos, G. A. title: Biologists May Have Discovered Two of the World’s Loudest Birds
content:
The red-legged sereima (above), which is a contender for the title of “world’s loudest bird” with the bare-throated bellbird (top of page). Credit: João Menezes
An unprecedented study of 123 bird species reveals clues about how some birds produce such powerful calls while leaving open the question of why extreme loudness evolved.
A bird can unleash a call loud enough to rival a jackhammer, yet measuring that blast in the wild is surprisingly difficult. Sound weakens as it travels, so a call that overwhelms a microphone nearby may barely register from farther away. For biologists trying to compare species scattered across different landscapes, that simple fact has made one basic question unusually hard to answer: just how loud can birds get?
Carrying a portable sound meter and a laser rangefinder into the field,
University of Massachusetts Amherst
biologist Jeff Podos and his former graduate student João C.T. Menezes set out to put reliable numbers on bird calls. Among the species they measured, the bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema stood out as two contenders for the world’s loudest bird. The study was published recently in
Evolution
Distance complicates every wild bird call
“Figuring out how loud a bird call is should be pretty easy in the lab,” says Menezes, who completed this research as part of graduate work at UMass Amherst. “But until very recently, it has been very challenging to do in the field, and there’s very little data to draw on.”
Measuring a bird’s call in the wild becomes difficult because loudness, or amplitude, changes depending on how far the microphone is from the animal. Researchers therefore need to know both the sound level and the bird’s distance at the moment it calls. Scientists can capture birds and test them under controlled laboratory conditions, but that approach quickly becomes impractical when comparing large numbers of species across countries.
“You have to get your boots on the ground,” says Podos, who accompanied Menezes in measuring the amplitudes of 123 birds in the areas around Amherst, Massachusetts, and across Brazil.
A male bare-throated. Credit: University of Massachusetts Amherst
Golfers and workplace safety specialists helped make that fieldwork possible, although neither group was designing equipment for ornithologists. Accurate laser rangefinders developed for golf allowed the researchers to pinpoint a bird’s distance, while portable, high-resolution sound meters could record the strength of its call. Used together, the devices gave Menezes and Podos a practical way to measure bird volume in the wild.
Moving from species to species, the researchers assembled reliable amplitude measurements for 123 species, including 113 whose call volumes had never been cataloged. “We’ve been able to vastly increase the number of species for which there is amplitude data,” says Podos. “This is basic, foundational research that no one else has managed to do on this scale, and it points to all sorts of other questions that would be fun to follow up.”
Bird calls span a 58-decibel range
Across those measurements, bird calls spanned a striking 58-decibel range. At the quieter end, a hummingbird registered about 64 decibels, roughly comparable to a normal conversation. At the other extreme, bare-throated bellbirds and red-legged seriemas climbed above 120 peak decibels, putting them at the very top of the species the researchers measured.
Podos had encountered such extreme volume before. In 2019,
he reported that the Amazon’s white bellbird produced the world’s loudest known bird call
, louder than standing next to a revving chainsaw. Guinness World Records later recognized the finding. Record-setting calls, however, are only a side effect of a much broader question that Podos and Menezes are trying to answer.
Comparing the bodies of the birds with their measured calls revealed some of the physical machinery behind extreme volume. Larger birds tended to be louder, possibly because their bulkier muscles allow them to compress and force out more air. Wider beak openings were also associated with louder calls, much as the broad bell of a trumpet helps project sound outward.
https://youtu.be/9r35UUlsS_8
A new contender for the world’s loudest bird: bare-throated bellbird. A male bare-throated bellbird sings in the Atlantic Forest of Brazil, near Macuquinho Lodge, Salesópolis, SP. Credit: João Menezes
Loudness defies the expected ecological patterns
While body size and beak width offered a physical explanation for loudness, the researchers found no similarly clear ecological pattern. Menezes and Podos had expected especially loud calls to appear more often in birds that were weak flyers, lived in dense forests, or practiced polygamy. Each idea offered a plausible advantage for shouting farther: limited mobility could make long-distance communication useful, thick vegetation could block visual signals, and mating calls that carry farther might reach more potential partners.
Instead, the measurements failed to produce clear, broad support for those predictions. Loudness could be linked to body size and beak opening, but the ecological and evolutionary reasons some birds became exceptionally loud remained much harder to pin down.
“We now know some of the hows,” says Menezes. “Bigger bodies and wider beaks, but we’ve yet to discover the whys, and we probably need much more data from many more species to be able to tease out what’s going on the ecological and evolutionary front.”
Back in the field, that unanswered question means more birds to find, more distances to measure, and more calls to catch at exactly the right moment. Podos is eager to return with Menezes, a golf rangefinder, and a sound meter in hand.
“Yogi Berra said ‘you can observe a lot by watching,’ and the world has some beautiful things to see,” says Podos. “You can’t do this kind of work in the lab, or by scraping data from the internet. You have to get out into the world, you have to pay careful attention to what you’re seeing and hearing, and anything you do in the field that forces you to observe more carefully is really fun—it takes you back to the roots of why we do science in the first place.”
Reference: “Evolutionary drivers of vocal amplitude in birds” by João C T Menezes and Jeffrey Podos, 29 September 2026,
Evolution
DOI: 10.1093/evolut/qpag153

title: Squid Skin May Work Like an Ear, Surprising New Research Suggests
content:
Scientists have discovered a much larger network of sensory hair cells across the squid’s body than previously known. Because damage to similar hair bundles in the human inner ear is a major cause of hearing loss, studying how squid build, maintain, and tune these structures could reveal why human hearing fails. Credit: Stock
Squid have hundreds more sensory cells than scientists realized, with hair bundles that may help explain how human hearing works and breaks down.
Water flowing over a squid’s head and arms brushes tiny past bundles of hair-like projections that help the animal sense movement around it. Scientists have known about these sensory structures for years, but they had only a partial picture of how widely this equipment was spread across the squid’s body.
Brian McDermott and his colleagues at
Case Western Reserve University
have now found hundreds more of the cells carrying these bundles, extending across the animal’s entire surface. Their research, published in
Current Biology
, includes the first complete map of squid lateral lines, arrays of sensory cells known as hair cells. The newly revealed network could give researchers another way to investigate the delicate structures that make human hearing possible.
Hearing depends on delicate hair bundles
Inside a human ear, sound vibrations reach the cochlea, a snail-shaped organ lined with thousands of hair cells. Each cell carries a bundle of tiny projections called stereocilia, which move in response to those vibrations. The cells send signals through the nervous system to the brain, where that movement becomes meaningful sound.
“Often, when a child is born deaf or a hearing person loses their hearing, it is the hair bundle that has been damaged,” said McDermott, an associate professor at the Case Western Reserve School of Medicine. “So, studying the squid’s hair bundle holds promise for understanding how hearing loss occurs.”
Laser light reveals squid’s hidden sensors
McDermott’s team, which included graduate and undergraduate students, conducted part of the research at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, through a three-year fellowship program focused on how squid hear. Working with them was Carsten Wolff, the laboratory’s associate director of Imaging Service and Imaging Scholar.
An image of a squid taken at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, using light sheet microscopy. Case Western Reserve University researchers discovered that squid have hair cells over their entire bodies, not just their heads and arms. Credit: Carsten Wolff
A thin sheet of laser light illuminated the squid tissue one plane at a time, allowing the researchers to assemble detailed, three-dimensional images while minimizing tissue damage. This technique, called light sheet microscopy, brought the previously unknown hair cells into view and allowed the team to trace the sensory network across the body.
“Squid are cephalopods with a diverse population of hair cells on the surface of their bodies, which may yield insights not only into how these fascinating animals detect water movement to survive, but also into how hearing and deafness occur in humans,” McDermott said.
Squid skin may work like an ear
The squid’s hair bundles also varied in length, a finding that strengthens the comparison with human hearing. In the human cochlea, taller bundles occur where low pitches are detected, while shorter bundles occur where high pitches are detected. Those differences help tune the cells to particular sound frequencies.
Fish lateral lines have hair bundles that do not vary in length, according to the researchers, making the squid’s varying bundles a potentially useful distinction. McDermott’s team interprets that variation as a sign that squid may regulate bundle length to detect different frequencies of water movement, much as human hair cells respond to different pitches. In that sense, the researchers suggest, a squid’s skin may function something like an ear.
The tiny bundles brushed by water across a squid’s body could therefore offer more than clues to how it senses its surroundings. They give researchers a newly mapped place to investigate how fragile sensory structures work, and how damage to their counterparts deep inside our ears can take sound away.
Reference: “An anatomical map of squid lateral lines” by Haoming Wang, Carsten Wolff, Nicolas Pintozzi, Anna-Maria Petriv and Brian M. McDermott, ,
Current Biology
DOI: 10.1016/j.cub.2026.07.056

title: Scientists Discover Groundbreaking Clues to Tissue Regrowth and “Immortality” in the Ocean
content:
The sea cucumber study reveals an unusual form of tissue regrowth, with detached fragments continuing to heal, reorganize, and grow for more than three years in natural seawater. Credit: Shutterstock
Sea cucumber tissue kept growing for more than three years after removal, surviving in seawater teeming with microbes.
Like Thing, the disembodied hand in The Addams Family, a severed piece of sea cucumber tissue kept living without the body it came from, prompting scientists to describe the animal as a “real-life zombie.” Weeks after being cut from a tube foot, the fragment appeared to be growing in seawater full of microbes, far from the sterile conditions usually needed to keep tissue cultures alive.
Scientists at Memorial University of Newfoundland followed up by placing tissue removed from the feet, main body, and tentacles of three sea cucumbers in flowing seawater. The animals belonged to
Psolus fabricii
, a cold-water species. Working with collaborators including Rachel Sipler, a senior research scientist at Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences, the team documented what happened to those fragments in a study published in
Science Advances
Microscopy image of an excised tube foot stained with 5-bromo-2′-deoxyuridine showing cell differentiation, with denser green coloring reflecting areas of more active cellular processes. Credit: Sara Jobson
The detached fragments, called explants, retained their structure and could move independently, while the researchers detected immune activity and tissue reorganization. More than three years after removal, the tissue remained active when the team ended the experiments to prepare the findings for publication.
Seawater may feed the mouthless fragments
Without a mouth to take in food, the fragments appeared to absorb amino acids directly from the seawater. These molecules, which cells use to build proteins, offered a possible source of nourishment for tissue separated from its animal.
“Natural seawater is just about the most microbially diverse, least clean approach we could take experimentally,” Sipler said. “Yet, that rich environment full of bacteria and all this organic matter was actually feeding them and allowing this tissue to heal and grow.”
Keeping “immortal” cell lines such as HeLa alive has enabled scientists to conduct long-term experiments since the mid-20th century. Those cells can continue dividing indefinitely, but the earlier tissue cultures described by the researchers depended on carefully maintained “axenic” conditions, meaning bacteria and other organisms were absent. The team reports this as the first known demonstration of discarded tissue surviving and growing over the long term outside those tightly controlled conditions.
A progression of tube foot tissue one year (top) versus several years (bottom) after excision showing increasing wound closure and healing at the wound site over time. Shifting colors from red to lighter white and pink reflects pigmented cells forming and consolidating aggregates of healthy tissue and the progression of transparent connective tissue. Credit: Sara Jobson
When many echinoderms lose tissue, they can regenerate it, and many members of this animal group also show little cellular aging. Sea cucumbers belong to that group, but researchers had generally expected their detached tissue to eventually die. How long the surviving fragments can remain viable is still an open question.
“We haven’t grown a new, complete sea cucumber yet, but we are seeing pretty stunning growth and diversification of cells literally years after this tissue was removed,” Sipler said. “It’s like a lizard that loses its tail. We know some lizards can grow new tails; we’re talking about whether the tail can grow a new lizard.”
Regeneration research with fewer laboratory barriers
“This discovery highlights that the ocean holds profoundly unexpected biological innovations,” said Gloucester Marine Genomics Institute Science Director Andrea Bodnar, who was not involved in the study. “The fact that tissue explants from a sea cucumber can heal, reorganize, and survive independently for years in natural seawater suggests an entirely new model for biological resilience and tissue regeneration.”
Culturing sea cucumber tissue could also give research and teaching laboratories a more accessible experimental model. The authors say it is easier to grow and, because it comes from an invertebrate, involves fewer research restrictions than human-based or other vertebrate cell lines. That could be useful where legal obstacles or limited biosafety infrastructure make those established models difficult to use.
Sipler, an oceanographer, credits “keen observation” with recognizing the significance of that discarded tube foot tissue, still growing in seawater weeks after removal. “The best advances in science are made when you find a natural analog for what you’re studying,” she said. “Here is this species that has this groundbreaking ability, and we had no idea. It’s a reminder how much is yet to be discovered in the marine environment, and how important it is to protect these resources that may hold really valuable knowledge for us.”
Reference: “Natural tissue immortality: Indefinite survival of sea cucumber explants” by Sara Jobson, Emaline M. Montgomery, Jean-François Hamel, Rachel E. Sipler and Annie Mercier, 27 May 2026,
Science Advances
DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeb1394
