title: Researchers Stretch a Quantum Material and Uncover Two Hidden Superconducting States
content:
CsV3Sb5 is an unusual quantum material known as a kagome metal, named for the interconnected triangular pattern of atoms in its crystal structure. Credit: Stock
Stretching a quantum material revealed two distinct superconducting states, challenging previous assumptions about its behavior and offering new clues to the mechanisms behind superconductivity.
Stretching a crystal by less than 1% has allowed scientists to separate two distinct superconducting states in a material that has puzzled physicists for years. The experiment also increased the temperature at which superconductivity begins, without substantially changing another form of electronic order within the crystal.
The findings could help settle a long-standing debate surrounding CsV3Sb5, an unusual metal whose superconducting properties have produced conflicting experimental results. By controlling strain along a single direction, researchers found a way to investigate superconductivity independently of the charge ordering that normally complicates its behavior.
Why This Unusual Metal Has Puzzled Physicists
CsV3Sb5 belongs to a family of materials called kagome metals, named for the distinctive pattern of interconnected triangles formed by their atomic structures. This geometry can produce unusual electronic behavior, including competing forms of quantum order.
At approximately 94 kelvin (−290°F), CsV3Sb5 develops a charge density wave, a periodic rearrangement of electronic charge. At much lower temperatures, around 2.5 kelvin (−455°F), it becomes superconducting, allowing electrical current to flow without resistance. Scientists have struggled to determine how these two states interact and what type of superconductivity the material supports.
One unresolved question concerns the superconducting gap, an energy gap associated with the pairing of electrons. Some experiments have suggested that this gap remains open throughout the material’s electronic structure, while others have indicated the presence of nodes, locations where the gap falls to zero. These possibilities point to different characteristics of the underlying superconducting state.
Stretching the Crystal Changes Its Superconductivity
To investigate, a team led by Associate Professor Shinji Kawasaki and Professor Guo-qing Zheng of Okayama University in Japan applied controlled strain to high-quality CsV3Sb5 crystals. Using a custom piezoelectric strain cell, they stretched or compressed the material along one crystallographic direction while monitoring its superconducting transition and local electronic properties through nuclear quadrupole resonance measurements.
A close-up of the piezoelectric-driven strain cell, hand-built by the research team, used to apply precise mechanical strain to single crystals of CsV3Sb5 while measuring their superconducting properties at low temperature. The apparatus enabled the discovery of two distinct, hidden superconducting states in the material. Credit: Associate Professor Shinji Kawasaki and Professor Guo-qing Zheng from Okayama University, Japan
Stretching produced a clear increase in the superconducting transition temperature. Without applied strain, superconductivity began at approximately 3.0 kelvin (−454°F). Under tensile strain of +0.90%, that temperature rose to 3.6 kelvin (−453°F). Compression did not produce the same enhancement.
The charge density wave, however, remained essentially unchanged. Unlike hydrostatic pressure, which can influence superconductivity by modifying charge order, uniaxial strain allowed the researchers to strengthen superconductivity while leaving the existing charge density wave largely intact.
Two Superconducting States Emerge Under Strain
At the highest tensile strain, the researchers detected two separate superconducting transitions. The first appeared at 3.6 kelvin and was associated with a nodal superconducting state. A second transition occurred at 3.0 kelvin and exhibited a nodeless state.
The measurements provide evidence for two superconducting states that are nearly degenerate under ordinary conditions, meaning their energies are very similar. Applying strain appears to separate these states, offering a possible explanation for why earlier experiments reached different conclusions about the material’s superconducting gap.
“For years, different measurements of CsV3Sb5 have pointed toward seemingly different superconducting states,” says Prof. Kawasaki. “Our results show that these states can coexist and that uniaxial strain can separate them, giving us a direct way to study each state.”
A New Way to Investigate Unconventional Superconductivity
The measurements also showed that tensile strain strengthened the unconventional nodal component. Its estimated contribution increased from approximately 10% without applied strain to about 26% at +0.90% strain, suggesting that stretching selectively favors this superconducting pairing channel.
“Strain gives us an independent control knob in this material—it enhances superconductivity without changing the bulk charge density wave,” says Prof. Kawasaki.
The approach could be extended to other unconventional superconductors in which multiple electronic orders coexist, including iron-based superconductors and heavy-fermion materials. Applying strain may help researchers distinguish the mechanisms responsible for superconductivity from the effects of competing charge or spin order.

title: Global guidelines set common test protocols for indoor solar cells, perovskites included
content:
Global guidelines set common test protocols for indoor solar cells, perovskites included
Researchers at Tor Vergata University of Rome and other institutions worldwide, more than 60 organizations in all, including universities, research centers, metrology institutes and companies from 22 countries, recently published a consensus set of best practices for measuring indoor solar cells. The aim is to make results from different labs comparable. Indoor photovoltaics (PV) power sensors, wearables and other IoT devices from ordinary lighting, but currently have no widely adopted test standard. Differences in light source, intensity and procedure can shift reported results by as much as 60% in relative terms for similar devices.
The guidelines recommend a single reference light source: a white LED with a 4,000 K color temperature as the future standard, with 5,000 K as the current one. A 2,700 K LED is suggested for devices aimed at homes. Performance should always be reported at 200 lux, with additional results at 1,000 and 50 lux for the best devices. The paper also covers how to set up and calibrate the test system, how to mask small cells, and how to report results, and it summarizes all of this in three checklists. For small lab cells, it recommends a mask opening of 75-80% of the active area to avoid overestimating the current.
The guidelines also cover stability, which the authors say previous practice had largely left unaddressed. They propose four tests: light soaking at 1,000 lux, dark storage, light-dark cycling and light soaking at higher intensities. Cells that don’t degrade quickly should be aged for at least 1,000 hours.
The study names perovskite, organic and dye-sensitized cells as new-generation indoor PV technologies. The paper cites lab-scale efficiencies of 30-45% indoors, compared with 7-16% for commercial amorphous silicon modules. Indoor perovskite efficiency claims are common, so a shared test method matters for comparing them.
“High laboratory efficiencies mean little if no two laboratories measure them the same way,” said first author Abhisek Chakraborty. The work was coordinated by Prof. Thomas M. Brown and Dr. Chakraborty of the Centre for Hybrid and Organic Solar Energy (CHOSE) at Tor Vergata.
The participating organizations are Tor Vergata University of Rome; TNO; Tsinghua University; Solertix; Halocell Europe; ENEA; Universitat Rovira i Virgili; Toin University of Yokohama; PHD Semicon Research (SENAI FIEMG Innovation and Technology Center); title: 仿冒知名品牌！超500万元侵权光伏产品被海关查获-索比光伏网
content:
据上海海关10日发布的数据，1月至9月，上海海关所属上海外高桥港区海关(以下简称外港海关)、洋山海关等口岸一线部门，累计查发涉嫌侵权光伏产品案16起，价值合计500余万元。
上海外港海关关员对一批侵权光伏产品进行查验。谢宗赢 摄
光伏产业是中国外贸“新三样”的核心品类，中国光伏组件产能占全球八成以上，是“中国制造”出海的一张亮眼名片。然而，部分不法分子觊觎行业市场红利，企图仿冒知名品牌光伏组件，以低价抢占海外市场、牟取非法利益。这些侵权产品不仅侵害企业商标权益、扰乱行业外贸秩序，更会损害“中国制造”的国际形象。
今年以来，上海海关持续强化知识产权海关保护力度，不断提升侵权打击精准度。“我们盯紧重点商品，利用商标智能识别工具，从包装做工、防伪标签、工艺细节等多维度辨真伪，把侵权产品外流的链条实实在在地掐断。”外港海关查验四科科长赵方逍说。
同时，上海海关还积极打通联动维权的“快车道”：主动引导权利人申请知识产权海关保护备案及总担保，简化逐票办理担保手续，让维权流程更简、成本更低；邀请品牌技术专家为口岸一线查验关员讲解最新仿冒手法和识别技巧，帮助关员练就识别侵权风险的“火眼金睛”。
上海海关与上海市知识产权局、浦东新区政府共同成立了“科创企业跨境知识产权服务工作站”，签订《知识产权协同保护共建协议》，明确9方面合作内容，就企业培训、案件查办、信息互通等工作打通知识产权协同保护全路径。目前，上海海关已围绕不同区域的业务特点和产业特色，创建知识产权海关保护工作站点4个，形成多点式、分散化、广覆盖的立体服务格局。
上海海关还联合南京、杭州等海关，定期开展长三角生态绿色一体化示范区知识产权保护共享交流，多方合力，为区域光伏企业出海织密知识产权保护网。

title: Hampidjan Advant awarded lifting equipment contract for East Anglia TWO
content:
Hampidjan Advant awarded lifting equipment contract for East Anglia TWO TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Hampidjan Advant awarded lifting equipment contract for East Anglia TWO
Cadeler has awarded Hampidjan Advant a contract to manufacture and supply
lifting slings for the 960 MW East
Anglia TWO offshore wind farm,
located off the Suffolk coast.
The contract marks a significant milestone for Hampidjan Advant and represents
one of the company’s largest single orders to date. The lifting slings
will be manufactured using high-modulus polyethylene (HMPE) fibre, which
is designed for demanding offshore wind lifting operations.
According to the company, the largest sling supplied for the project will
measure 190 mm in diameter and 64 metres in length.
Under the agreement, the lifting solutions will be deployed aboard Cadeler’s
offshore installation vessel, Wind Ace, supporting the company’s transport
and installation activities for the project.
East Anglia TWO is owned by ScottishPower Renewables and, once operational,
will comprise 75 wind turbines capable of generating enough electricity
to power around 950,000 homes annually.
The agreement further strengthens the relationship between Hampidjan Advant
and Cadeler, following their previous collaboration on the Hornsea

title: KING THREE vessel to support Nordseecluster B operations
content:
Dajin Heavy Industry's KING THREE, a 40,000 DWT special deck carrier, has
departed from the company's Tangshan manufacturing base on its maiden voyage
carrying 10 monopiles for the Nordseecluster
B offshore wind project
in the German North Sea.
The vessel is travelling to Eemshaven in the Netherlands. The shipment
marks the vessel's first operational deployment and completes the commissioning
of Dajin's three vessel KING series fleet.
According to the company, the addition of the third vessel enables it to
manage ocean transport using its own fleet, supporting the delivery of
offshore wind components and reducing reliance on external shipping capacity.
The monopiles were fabricated at Dajin's Tangshan offshore wind production
facility. The company said the site features an enclosed production line
designed to support continuous manufacturing regardless of weather conditions.
Dajin stated that the integration of manufacturing, port operations, ocean
transport and overseas delivery forms part of its strategy to provide end
to end services for offshore wind projects.

title: OEG awarded temporary power contract by Ørsted
content:
OEG has been awarded a contract by Ørsted to provide temporary power services
for the 2.9 GW Hornsea
3 offshore wind farm,
located 160 km off the Yorkshire coast.
The contract will provide temporary power during offshore converter station
commissioning, as well as the turbine installation and commissioning phases.
OEG will supply power onboard a jack-up vessel using five 200 kVA generators
and two 300 kVA generators. The solution is designed to deliver temporary
power requirements of up to 1,400 kVA while minimising the equipment footprint
on the transition piece.
Rob Williams, technical manager for OEG’s temporary power team, said:
“We have been working closely with the Ørsted construction management
team over the last few months to ensure we provide the correct bespoke
technical solutions in support of this exciting new project.”
The contract builds on the companies’ existing relationship, with OEG's
temporary power teams supporting both Hornsea 1 and Hornsea 2 projects.

title: Scottish Renewables calls for action to unlock Scotland’s port potential
content:
Scottish Renewables calls for action to unlock Scotland’s port potential TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Scottish Renewables calls for action to unlock Scotland’s port potential
Scottish Renewables has called for action to help unlock the full potential
of Scotland’s ports, warning that infrastructure and energy related barriers
could hinder their ability to support the growing offshore wind sector.
The new report, Port Power – Electricity Demand in Scotland, outlines
the changing electricity requirements of Scottish ports as they take on
a greater role in offshore wind development.
Scottish ports support offshore wind projects through manufacturing and
assembly activities, industrial electrification and maritime decarbonisation.
Significant investment has already been made across the sector, including
£1.45 million in expansion funding for Montrose Port.
However, Scottish Renewables said grid constraints, consenting delays and
high electricity costs risk undermining these investments.
The organisation is calling for port electricity demand to be reflected
in the Strategic Spatial Energy Plan (SSEP) and Regional Energy Strategic
Plans (RESPs) to ensure future energy infrastructure aligns with industry
The report highlighted four key findings based on interviews with representatives
ranging from incremental capacity increases for existing operations to
substantial new demand from industrial tenants.
According to the report, limited network capacity, high upfront costs,
electricity prices and uncertainty over future vessel demand are also restricting
progress across the sector.
To address these barriers, Scottish Renewables is calling for faster grid
consenting, greater cost certainty, energy planning that reflects port
requirements, and connection reforms that better support future development.

title: New Zealand opens first offshore feasibility permit applications
content:
The New Zealand Government has announced the country’s first offshore
renewable energy feasibility permit application round under its new offshore
renewable energy regime.
The round will allow developers to apply for feasibility permits covering
designated areas offshore Taranaki and offshore Waikato/South Auckland.
A feasibility permit enables developers to undertake studies and assess
the viability of a potential offshore wind development within a specified
permit area.
Developers that complete feasibility work will be required to obtain a
commercial permit, along with any other necessary consents, before they
can construct and operate an offshore renewable energy project.

further details on eligibility requirements, the application process, assessment

content:
Ørsted has announced the acquisition of the remaining 49.9% stake in the
Gunfleet
1 and 2 offshore wind farms, located off the coast of Essex, giving the
company full ownership of the assets.
The company exercised a longstanding buyback right established under the

closing conditions.

in August 2009 and entered commercial operation in 2010.
Richard Bodal Hansen, Ørsted's UK country manager, said: "Taking full
ownership gives us greater flexibility to shape the site's future and build
on the value of an asset we know well."

to power around 125,000 UK homes annually.

energy portfolio and expands its ownership across its UK offshore wind

title: OpenAI’s Plan To Revive Sora
content: Remember OpenAI’s video model Sora and all the great Sam Altman memes that came from it? Earlier this year, the ChatGPT-maker canned both the model and the TikTok-like app it powered as part of broader culling of server-intensive “side projects” even as rivals xAI and Google forged ahead with their own video models. Well, there’s a chance that a version of Sora is coming back from the dead. A stealthy startup developing AI video for filmmakers, which we revealed last month, is in talks with OpenAI to access Sora, tweak it and sell software or other services using it, according to a person with knowledge of the talks. Hollywood mogul Jeffrey Katzenberg , former Sora research lead Bill Peebles , and former Dropbox CFO Sujay Jaswa co-founded the startup in recent months . (We don’t know the startup’s name). It’s not clear whether the startup will get access to Sora’s weights, the “settings” that determine how the model responds to queries, but if the deal were to go through, the startup would get deep enough access to the model to heavily customize it, the person said. (AI developers like OpenAI tend to guard their model weights very closely, but in this case, sharing weights or other sensitive information wouldn’t be surprising when you consider that Peebles previously led Sora and already knows how the model works and was trained.) If a deal gets completed, OpenAI would receive equity in the new startup, this person said, though the amount couldn’t be learned. Working with Peebles makes a lot of sense, given how much money and time OpenAI spent developing Sora. The cost of making and running Sora was so high that the company decided to shift resources to its traditional large language models and ChatGPT, which are more economically viable. The new deal means OpenAI can salvage some sort of return on its Sora investment. OpenAI had abandoned Sora as part of a push to cut side projects and remain focused on ChatGPT and fighting Anthropic in the coding and enterprise fronts. In recent months, there’s been signs that OpenAI has backslid a bit on that push. It has revived efforts in robotics, hired a Patreon co-founder to lead a new “creator product” division, and it is also pushing hard on a costly personal-device initiative. Here’s what else is going on… Big Number OpenAI recently told investors that its annualized revenue was approaching $50 billion at the end of September, according to a person with knowledge of the communications. That’s around $20 billion less than revenue figures disclosed in other recent reports, including The Information's. Overheard The U.S. government is limiting Microsoft ’s ability to sponsor visas for certain immigrant workers, Vice President J.D. Vance said Thursday, citing an “ongoing investigation” into claims that Microsoft laid off Americans while continuing to hire more immigrants. Top executives at AI companies including Anthropic and OpenAI are gaming out scenarios for public revolt that could follow a catastrophic AI event, Axios reported. Anthropic said Friday that its AI used the internet to inadvertently fill out government forms and submit a false homicide crime tip to police. In response, Trump administration officials said they are now mandating AI companies to report and correct security incidents. The three safety researchers whom OpenAI fired last week challenged OpenAI ’s decision, saying on Thursday they were punished for raising safety concerns. The perpetrator of a recent hack of South Korean financial institutions that resulted in data leaks used an open-source Chinese AI agent called Artex and Chinese large language models, according to CrowdStrike . It is now exploring a $2 billion to $3 billion private funding round with existing investors instead. The Information first reported on the round here . Nuvacore , a six-month-old chip startup with no product yet that's designing a new type of central processor for data centers, is raising hundreds of millions of dollars at a valuation of roughly $2.5 billion, Reuters reported. GlobalFoundries signed a $2 billion, five-year manufacturing agreement with TSMC to produce silicon interposers — a packaging component used in AI chips — at its Malta, New York facility. Nvidia committed $1 billion over five years to expand the US's capacity for “super intelligence” research and development, funding work in quantum computing, healthcare and energy at national laboratories and universities. Arena , formerly known as Chatbot Arena , which runs a leaderboard that ranks AI models, raised $200 million in a Series B funding round co-led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Khosla Ventures. Veir , which makes superconducting power-delivery systems for AI data centers, raised $110 million in a Series C funding round co-led by Matter Venture Partners and Tyche Partners. Ultra , a warehouse-robotics startup that rents out robots on a subscription basis, disclosed $62 million in total funding—a $50 million Series A led by Framework Ventures plus an earlier $12 million seed led by Y Combinator —and deepened its partnership with Physical Intelligence to supply AI software for its robots. Hone , founded by former OpenAI and Cognition staffers to build AI agents that can run entire business operations rather than single tasks, raised $60 million in seed funding led by Benchmark and Index Ventures. Sabi , which is building a baseball cap lined with roughly 100,000 non-contact neural sensors that converts brain signals into prompts for AI systems, raised $50 million in seed funding led by Khosla Ventures. title: How Microsoft’s New Office Chief Fixed Copilot and Won Over Nadella
content: In the summer of 2025, Microsoft was fielding customer complaints that its AI assistant, Copilot, was buggy and not good enough at automating work in Excel or PowerPoint. In response, Charles Lamanna, then a Microsoft president and rising star within the giant firm, went to CEO Satya Nadella with a bold proposal: Microsoft needed to consider paying for AI models from Anthropic to make Copilot work better. “At the time, that was heresy,” Lamanna said in an interview. The idea was met with skepticism from other Microsoft executives, like Judson Althoff, Microsoft’s commercial chief, according to another Microsoft employee with knowledge of the situation. Althoff pointed out that Anthropic models would be far pricier than OpenAI’s, which Microsoft can use at no additional cost thanks to its close partnership with OpenAI . But Lamanna won over Nadella with demos showing that Anthropic’s models were then better at mathematical tasks needed in Excel and creating aesthetically pleasing PowerPoints. “We pushed back because if you have a belief or a thesis, you just have to go all the way with it,” said Lamanna, 38. Months later, Nadella gave Lamanna oversight of thousands of developers working on Copilot, streamlining what was a messy collection of separate engineering teams. Now, just over a year later, Lamanna’s bet on revamping Copilot’s innards appears to have paid off. Customers such as AT&T say they have noticed improvements in Copilot over the past year. While Microsoft remains in an existential battle to win over enterprise customers as AI reorders the power dynamics of the industry, Copilot’s corporate users have more than doubled since the start of the year to over 30 million now. Meanwhile, Lamanna’s profile has continued to expand within Microsoft. In March, Nadella appointed Lamanna to a new role as executive vice president overseeing Copilot engineering, reporting directly to him. (Lamanna shares oversight of Copilot with executive vice president Jacob Andreou). And earlier this month, Nadella put him in charge of Office, making Lamanna responsible for Microsoft’s flagship software. That move follows the July retirement of Rajesh Jha, an executive vice president who’d been responsible for Office and Windows, among other things. Lamanna also oversees Microsoft’s Teams business, and altogether, his organization consists of around 25,000 people, more than triple the number of employees he oversaw a year ago. (Microsoft has over 220,000 employees; its largest divisions are its sales and Azure cloud units, each of which has more than 60,000 full-time employees). Multiple senior Microsoft executives say they now see Lamanna as a potential successor to Nadella as Microsoft’s next CEO. Like Nadella, Lamanna is seen as a wonk and as someone who likes to sink into technical engineering details. While he isn’t thought of as a charismatic salesman type, insiders say his ability to unify growing teams has impressed Nadella. The two meet weekly. Over the past year, Nadella has brought Lamanna to Microsoft’s quarterly board meetings—along with a few other executives like Andreou, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, security chief Hayete Gallot and executive vice president Arun Ulag, who oversees Azure’s database products. Some senior Microsoft execs see Nadella’s decision to include these executives as a concerted effort to introduce the board to a range of possible successors. The pressure on Lamanna is substantial. He has to develop products that can convince corporate customers to spend more on Microsoft’s AI and productivity software even as companies are increasingly scrutinizing every dollar of their AI budgets. A year after adding Anthropic models to Copilot, Lamanna is now focused on optimizing Copilot and ensuring it can choose the right mix of models for the right tasks in a way that minimizes cost without sacrificing quality. Doing so is crucial for Microsoft to stay competitive in how much it charges for Office and other products amid a sea of alternatives, including products from Anthropic and OpenAI. Lamanna finds himself navigating a complicated landscape in which Anthropic and OpenAI are both key Microsoft business partners—and also fierce rivals. Lamanna has told staff that Microsoft should be “the Costco of AI,” the place everyone—from broke college students to millionaires—goes for AI products because it offers the best value at the best price. “We’re not going to be some boutique that only the top coders and the top R&D folks in the world get to access at a huge price,” Lamanna said. “We’re going to drive all these prices down, so everyone can enjoy it.” Jacob Andreou speaking at a Windows event last week. Photo by Heather Diehl/Getty Images From Intern to Top Brass Lamanna has spent his entire career in Microsoft’s orbit. His first job at the company came nearly two decades ago when, as a University of Notre Dame undergrad, he landed a software engineering internship working on OneCare, a now-defunct antivirus program for Windows PCs. After graduating in 2009, he continued as a software engineer in Microsoft’s then-nascent cloud unit before leaving in 2012 to co-found MetricsHub, an enterprise software startup, which Microsoft acquired for an undisclosed sum a year later. That deal brought Lamanna back to the company. In the decade that followed, Lamanna steadily moved up in the cloud unit led by Scott Guthrie, eventually taking over Microsoft’s business applications group, which includes its Dynamics 365 customer relationship management software and low-code app builder Power Apps. While leading those teams, Lamanna said he tried to break from the company’s notoriously cutthroat culture by implementing a “no jerks” policy within his unit, a change that was “very much needed” 10 years ago, a point in time when Microsoft was known for a brutal ranking system that pitted employees against each other and led to company infighting. Lamanna also tried to cut out some of Microsoft’s management bureaucracy by working directly with engineering teams, writing his own code and moving quickly to turn junior staff’s good ideas into products Microsoft could market to customers. After several years leading Microsoft’s business apps group, Lamanna last June was moved into a new role reporting to Jha. At the time, Lamanna’s official purview was still business applications, but by last summer he began taking more ownership of Copilot within Jha’s org. At the time, disparate groups across Windows and Office were building separate Copilot features that would appear in different Microsoft applications. Jha would reward the groups whose Copilot features were quickly adopted by customers by adding those features to every version of Copilot. It was a tangled mess, employees said, and some executives across the company grumbled that the setup led to infighting and divisions claiming credit for other engineers’ work. Then came Lamanna’s pitch to Nadella to add Anthropic models, a change that affected Copilot across all of its applications. The shift was critical, Lamanna said, because Copilot’s design had previously assumed it would only rely on one model maker—OpenAI—rather than being able to work well with a range of models. “It would be dangerous if we built Copilot for too long assuming model monogamy, because you basically would, like, bake in too much dependence on that model’s behaviors—it would become very hard in the future to ever add new models,” Lamanna said. By March, Jha announced his plans to step down from the company, and Nadella unified all of the disparate engineering groups working under Lamanna on the systems behind Copilot. The new structure was a relief to some engineers, according to current and former employees, who say Lamanna’s leadership has felt more like a single unit moving towards cohesive goals. His staff have also praised his willingness to move quickly and elevate good ideas by his reports regardless of their seniority. “If we just stuck with the way we were doing things, we would have fallen behind,” said Soufiane Loukili, a vice president of engineering in Lamanna’s unit. “[Lamanna] wouldn’t wait for a formal review or a large process to go through. He would push us to try new things with a calculated tolerance for risk, and it worked.” Getting Customers Bang for their Buck In his current role, Lamanna is now focused on convincing enterprise customers to spend more on Microsoft’s AI software every quarter while continuing to make Copilot less expensive. After Microsoft began adding Anthropic models last fall, a group of engineers in the Office division developed “agent mode,” a feature that steers AI models from both OpenAI and Anthropic to spend more time reasoning when automating tasks in Office that Microsoft started previewing last fall. While customers previously had to manually turn on agent mode, Lamanna found that agent mode worked better for nearly every task. By this spring, he had overhauled Copilot to make agent mode the default. Soon after, Microsoft saw a sharp increase in internal customer satisfaction data, according to someone familiar with the situation. Customers say they have noticed an uptick in Copilot’s quality. Since Microsoft rolled out agent mode, AT&T employees have been relying on Copilot for the “lion’s share” of their automation of personal productivity work, said AT&T VP Mark Austin. The company increased its number of Copilot licenses over the past year and now has around 18,000 seats, AT&T said. The recent improvement may not be enough to win over every customer. Nimesh Mehta, chief information officer at National Life Group, said his employees started testing Copilot back in 2023 and found it to be essentially “useless.” But when his team tested it again this spring, they found it had improved markedly, Mehta said. Still, Mehta said most of the company’s employees use ChatGPT. He hasn’t been convinced to switch back to Copilot. Judson Althoff speaks on stage during We Day in 2015. Photo by Mat Hayward/Getty Images “The interface still isn’t perfect, but it’s much better overall,” Mehta said. “Still, since it left such a sour taste in our users’ perspectives, they are not willing to give it another shot.” More recently, improving Copilot’s gross margins while keeping customers happy has been a top priority for Lamanna, according to someone with knowledge of the situation. Over the past six months, as the capabilities of OpenAI models have caught back up to Anthropic’s, Lamanna has directed staff to program Copilot to rely more on OpenAI models for “agent mode,” which has improved the product’s margins because Microsoft can run OpenAI models for free, this person said. Lamanna has also pushed teams in recent months to improve Copilot’s efficiency in other ways. Engineers in his unit developed a model router—software that picks between models—using a homegrown LLM that chooses the cheapest model to complete a task without sacrificing quality. The vast majority of people using Copilot in Office use its “auto” mode that lets the router select models automatically, which has also improved margins, this person said. While Microsoft’s payments to Anthropic to power Copilot for its customers have grown this year—it is on track to pay Anthropic more than $2 billion a year —swapping in OpenAI models for “agent mode” and other advanced features has helped temper that growth even as more people use Copilot, this person said. Lamanna has also spearheaded products like Microsoft’s Copilot Cowork features in Office, which resembles Anthropic’s Claude Cowork, an AI tool that can handle complex tasks on a computer like managing files. Another Lamanna effort was Autopilot AI agent, which was based on the viral success of OpenClaw. With AutoPilot, Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot a more useful “always-on” agent that can also use tools from other vendors like Workday, so that Microsoft’s software becomes the default place for people to do the majority of their work. Lamanna and Omar Shahine, a Microsoft vice president who leads the team developing AutoPilot, talk daily about new tools that they’re experimenting with, like Meta’s Muse and Instinct’s AI agents, Shahine said. Using outside tools is unorthodox at Microsoft, which has historically encouraged employees to solely use the company’s own products. Shahine looks at it as a necessity. “I think that’s really important because the industry is going through a huge change right now,” he said. Lamanna’s test now is to continue to accelerate Copilot’s growth while convincing corporate customers to spend more money on Microsoft’s existing bundle of Office, Windows and security software. Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft, during an event in San Francisco last week. Photo by David Paul Morris/Getty Images A key step in that vision launched last week when Microsoft launched its revamped Copilot super-app that rolled together 365 Copilot with additional features like Autopilot and Copilot Cowork, which will cost customers extra based on how much they use the features. If Lamanna realizes that vision, it would be a career win that could burnish his credentials as a successor to Nadella, should the CEO decide he’s ready to move on. Lamanna, who hasn’t served as a CEO since founding his startup more than a decade ago, hasn’t ruled out the possibility of helming a company once again. “I mean, I’d say in the abstract, yes,” he said when asked whether he’d ever like to be a CEO again. “But right now, I’m having quite a bit of fun making Copilot be the best product for the best price for all of our customers.”

title: Amazon’s Bargains Include Its Stock
content: It’s the quiet before the storm of earnings season, which starts in a week or two. While we wait for the third-quarter updates, here’s a thought: Investor enthusiasm for semiconductor stocks and blue-sky vision companies like SpaceX appears to have sucked money out of stocks of long-established tech companies. Some are now trading at bargain-basement prices. We’re thinking specifically of Amazon, whose stock really deserves a bit more love. We know the gripes: Like Alphabet and Meta, Amazon is spending an absolute ton—$220 billion this year alone—on capital expenditures to build out its AI data center capacity. That’s not without risk, for sure: The investment depends on business demand for AI services taking off. Even so, that can’t justify Amazon trading at a discount to Walmart, as it has done for the last 18 months or so. Walmart is expected to grow revenue this year by about 5.6%—about a third of Amazon’s estimated growth rate. And yet Amazon is trading at about 29 times forward earnings, compared with 37 times for Walmart, according to Koyfin data. Moreover, while Walmart is a predominantly brick-and-mortar grocery store chain, Amazon has a much more diverse business. It owns the dominant online shopping service, where its retail sales alone grew 13% in the first half. It’s also the biggest cloud provider and a major film and television business. And it’s got a bunch of other bits and pieces, including its nascent Leo satellite service, which is trying to compete with SpaceX in satellite-delivered broadband. It’s not hard to make the case that with a market capitalization of $2.8 trillion, Amazon is a bit undervalued. Consider this math: AWS should be worth at least $1 trillion, if not much more, given its expected growth in the next couple of years and where small neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius are trading. The film and TV studio business should be worth at least as much as Netflix, which has a market capitalization of $300 billion. Then there’s the shopping business, including merchant services, ads and subscriptions. They’re all tied together in various ways, which complicates things. Online sales and merchant services, excluding ads and subscriptions, generated revenue of $468 billion in the 12 months to June, growing at about 12%, which means it could hit $500 billion this year.  If you apply Amazon’s forward revenue multiple of 3.3 to that number, the online shopping side is worth about $1.7 trillion. Then there’s the ad business, which is an $80 billion a year business right now, growing at 20% to 25% annually. It’s mostly promotional spending for merchants on Amazon’s platform, which makes it less valuable than ads on Meta or Google, but it should still add hundreds of millions in value to Amazon. There’s upside elsewhere. At Goldman Sachs’ recent Communicopia conference, tech analyst Eric Sheridan made the case that Amazon should be among the best-positioned companies to benefit from the rise of robots, helping automate more of the logistics and delivery parts of its shopping business and improving profit margins. Of course, there are lots of variables, even aside from the uncertainty about the return on the AWS capex outlay. We don’t know how the rise of AI agents will change consumer behavior, if at all. If agent traffic largely replaces humans scrolling on Amazon, its ad business could be wiped out. To be sure, Amazon’s status as a conglomerate likely dooms its stock to always trade at a discount to its real value. It’s possible that one day the company will break up into two or three pieces, with AWS the most logical business to be carved off. That day is a ways off, however, as AWS needs cash flow flowing from the shopping business to finance its capex right now. But even the possibility of a breakup points up the opportunity for investors with a long term time horizon. Anthropic’s Rogue Agents AI agents seem to have a good imagination, if not a sense of humor. That’s one conclusion from Anthropic’s blog post on Friday which detailed new “examples of unintended model actions” it had observed during evaluations of Claude. One example, which drew some attention over the weekend, was prompted by Claude being told to run some tasks on “randomly selected webpages.” The model “landed on a page referencing an unsolved homicide; that page contained a tip form run by a police department.” Claude had been instructed “never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases or submit anything destructive, but the instructions did not rule out form submissions.” So Claude “filled out the form with the following: ‘I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around” the street in question…please contact me if this information is relevant.” The submission was flagged as spam and never forwarded for investigation. Still, you have to marvel at Claude’s ability to act like a drunken teenager. In Other News • SoftBank Group CEO Masayoshi Son is looking to raise up to $100 billion from Gulf investors to finance his AI investments, The Financial Times reported. • Firmus Grid, an AI cloud company backed by Nvidia, has pulled what would have been Australia’s biggest initial public offering in almost 30 years. The Sydney-based company had planned to raise nearly $5 billion at a valuation above $30 billion. It cited market volatility and said it will seek private funding instead. • Nuclear reactor startup Valar Atomics says it has sued one of its early backers, Day One Ventures, in Delaware court after shutting out the venture firm from its recent $1 billion funding round. Founders rarely sue their own investors, but Valar is asking the court to declare that the startup acted properly, after Day One refused to give up its right to invest in the Sequoia Capital-led funding round. title: How to Get Your Data Center Approved? Behave Like An Oil Company
content: AI data centers might be encountering a lot less community pushback in the U.S. if their developers thought of their projects like oilfields and spread the expected coming windfall much more freely, says Brian Janous, co-founder of Cloverleaf Infrastructure. Opposition in the U.S. to AI data centers has exploded, becoming a key hot-button issue animating the Nov. 3 midterm elections. A September poll by The New York Times found that 61% of likely voters oppose data center construction, and The Information has tracked at least 550 states and localities that have active data center moratoriums in place. Consequently, candidates in both red and blue states are racing to save their campaigns by trying to appear tough in confronting such projects. Janous, whose firm develops data centers, spoke on a panel I moderated last week for The Information on data centers. He argued that cloud firms and data center developers should cut communities in on the massive profits they expect over the coming decades. Developers will spend almost $3 trillion on the AI data center buildout in the U.S. by 2030, according to McKinsey . Janous cited oil development in Alaska, where since the 1970s oil companies have paid out some $31 billion to the state’s residents as their share of North Slope profits. The split is even richer in oil-producing countries such as Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan, where Western oil companies pay 80% of profits to the countries. The most pragmatic oil industry veterans don’t regard such payments as generosity but as a way to keep the peace. Oil projects can earn hundreds of billions of dollars in profit over a 30-year period, making payments to local communities a reasonable price to pay. While tech companies such as Microsoft, Meta and Amazon have talked up the benefits their data centers bring to local communities, they have doled out only tens of millions of dollars for accouterments like workforce training and recreation centers. At the higher end of the scale, though still relatively modest, was Amazon’s offer this month to invest $1 billion across the communities that host its data centers. There is also Hazle Township, Pa., where NorthPoint Development, a Missouri industrial project developer, during the summer offered residents $10,000 each to support the construction of a new data center. None of that will cut it, Janous said. “Communities really have to feel like they won a lottery by having a data center,” he said. “I liken it to the old company town. People should feel like, ‘Hey, we’re excited that Anthropic’s here because our community is a lot better off.’” The change in public reception to data centers has bubbled up relatively quickly: Over the last year, gripes surfaced about soaring electric bills, the use of sometimes-scarce water supplies, dust and noise. In recent months, however, those have spiraled into the moratoriums. Many industry veterans attribute the increased public opposition to anxiety about AI itself, as leaders of the biggest AI companies release increasingly alarming predictions that—among other things—AI will end the human race. The pushback has been international. There is resistance to new data centers and outright bans in South Korea, Singapore, Finland, Scotland, the Netherlands, Malaysia and many other countries. Allan Schurr, chief commercial officer at Enchanted Rock, which installs microgrids that provide power to data centers while they await a connection to the grid, suggested that developers could attract some local acceptance by offering power to communities amid worsening grid reliability in many places. Another panelist, William Mao, vice president of energy infrastructure at Delta Electronics, said data centers could provide power in the case of a catastrophic event like a hurricane or earthquake. “The data center power could be redirected to help stabilize the grid,” he said. Schurr pointed out that data center developers were taking steps to ensure communities were not being burdened by data center projects. “I know of no data centers that are trying to not pay their own way,” he said. Of course, it would be tricky for cloud firms to promise massive amounts to local communities since they don’t know when their investments would begin to pay off. But that’s not dissimilar to the oil companies, whose investments in oilfields also take years to deliver profits. The oil companies typically open the cash spigot to the countries in which they’re operating only after the capital expenses of oilfield development are paid off, which can take up to a decade. Janous’ point, though, was that the psychology of the AI buildout needed to change because communities are angry. “I think that’s what‘s driving a lot of this angst is the feeling like, ‘Hey, you know, what are we really getting out of this? We’re gonna make a bunch of tech companies richer, but are we gonna get to participate in some of this upside?’" he said. ---- Noteworthy China agreed to halve its exports of hybrid electric cars to the EU. The agreement Friday follows an export surge of Chinese-made hybrids and plug-in hybrids to Europe as vehicle sales of the major European carmakers have fallen dramatically . title: The Download: moon city problems and drone traffic controllers
content:
The Download: moon city problems and drone traffic controllers
Plus: An Anthropic AI model submitted a fake tip about an unsolved murder.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp.
A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining.
That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.
Find out what stands in the way of a city on the moon.
—Robin George Andrews
This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get your hands on a copy as soon as it lands on Wednesday 21 October!
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Brimstone and its one-stop process for making cleaner cement and critical minerals
Brimstone is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.
Brimstone is a code-switching climate tech company for these polarized political times. The US startup is part green cement company, part critical mineral producer.
During the Biden administration, its primary pitch was cement that generates about 60% fewer greenhouse-gas emissions. It achieves this by switching to silicate rocks instead of standard limestone, which releases carbon dioxide when heated.
Under the Trump administration, however, the company is emphasizing another benefit of its process: the ability to extract valuable materials from those same rocks.
Discover how it’s making strides on two industrial problems.
—James Temple
Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from geothermal power plants to smart turbines and semi-solid-state cells.
Job titles of the future: Delivery drone air traffic controller
The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,” he says. “I just immediately wanted to be a part of it.”
Wischnewsky is now an RPIC, or remote pilot in command, at a company called FlyTrex. An RPIC is like an air traffic controller. But instead of airplanes, they oversee fleets of drones that ferry cargo to homes and businesses
Here’s what it takes to become a drone air traffic controller.
—Eamon Whalen
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 An Anthropic AI model submitted a fake tip about an unsolved murder
The tip was in a new group of rogue actions Anthropic disclosed. (NYT $)
+ Police criticised the company for waiting nine days to report it after finding it. (WSJ $)
+ Another model submitted real government forms. (Quartz)
+ The White House has made AI incident reporting mandatory. (Axios)
+ But who’s liable when AI agents go rogue? (MIT Technology Review)
2 Ukraine’s drone strikes have dealt a major blow to Russian AI
Sunday’s attack shut down the third Yandex data centre hit in days. (Reuters $)
+ The strikes have disrupted Russia’s AI, cloud services, and apps. (Gizmodo)
+ They followed Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers. (Ars Technica)
+ Russian military satellites could disrupt Starlink. (Reuters $)
+ Ukraine’s drone data is fueling a wild market. (MIT Technology Review)
3 Iranian ChatGPT users have planted AI-generated articles in news outlets
About a dozen outlets ran roughly 100 articles by fake journalists. (CNN)
+ The articles criticised the Iran war’s effects on Americans. (WP $)
+ AI has been used to turn the Iran conflict into theatre. (MIT Technology Review)
4 Tesla has renamed “Full Self-Driving” as “Assisted Driving” in Europe
EU lawmakers said the old name was misleading.  (TechCrunch)
+ Tesla hopes the rebrand leads regulators to approve the feature. (Wired $)
+ Back in the US, it plans to increase toxic emissions near a school. (SFGate)
5 A ransomware negotiator has been arrested amid a hacking crackdown
The FBI suspects he was involved with a gang that recently claimed to have stolen data on the bureau’s employees. (Reuters $)
+ AI is making online crimes easier. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Hollywood's hottest villain right now is the tech billionaire
Four new films feature dark depictions of Silicon Valley leaders. (Axios $)
+ The real Mark Zuckerberg has also become a new character. (NYT $)
7 A new experiment is testing the Amazon’s response to rising CO₂
CO₂-releasing towers will simulate future atmospheric conditions. (Nature)
+ Is carbon removal in trouble? (MIT Technology Review)
8 The US hybrid boom has pushed some used car prices above new ones
Buyers are paying a premium to skip the wait for new models. (Wired $)
9 A new technology switches tattoos on and off with light
It can make permanent ink invisible. (New Scientist $)
10 Scientists spotted the most distant signal yet from the ancient universe
It could help them understand how the universe has evolved. (404 Media)
Quote of the day
“Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI.”
—Microsoft's president, Brad Smith, tells the BBC why AI urgently needs more regulations, including requiring firms to write "incident reports" and tell victims if the technology goes rogue.
One more thing
Geoffrey Hinton tells us why he’s now scared of the tech he helped build
Geoffrey Hinton is a pioneer of deep learning who helped develop some of the most important techniques at the heart of modern artificial intelligence, but after a decade at Google, he’s stepped down to focus on concerns he now has about AI.
Hinton is now spending his time on what he describes as “more philosophical work.” And that will focus on the small but—to him—very real danger that AI will turn out to be a disaster. Here’s why he’s so worried.
—Will Douglas Heaven
